utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth, to the interpreters; good morning to the legal assistants, court reporters. I think that Mr. Cayley, Mr. McCloskey, and all the Prosecution are there, so is the Defence. Good morning, General Krstic. We are continuing our hearing from yesterday, and we shall take up where we left off. Good morning, Mr. Ruez. As you know, you shall now be answering questions put to you by the Defence. And I see Mr. Petrusic on his feet. Mr. Petrusic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours; good morning to my learned colleagues of the Prosecution and good morning to you, Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, in the course of your testimony yesterday, you spoke about the units, that is to say, the commanders of the Drina Corps. You mentioned the special police force as well. My question for you is the following: The special police force, with its headquarters in Janja, whose deputy commander was Ljubisa Borovcanin, did that unit, the unit of the Ministry of the Internal Affairs of Republika Srpska, was it that unit, did it belong to that Ministry?

utterances.speaker: Jean-Rene Ruez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: Jean-Rene Ruez [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. That's fine. The 65th Protection Regiment, which you also mentioned as being in Nova Kasaba, was that a unit of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska as well?

utterances.speaker: Jean-Rene Ruez [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ruez, I apologise but could you please switch your other microphone on as well. Thank you. That's fine now. Thank you very much. It's on, I see. The microphone is on and functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The videotape that we saw yesterday and the contents of that video was an interview of General Krstic. Was that videotape, according to your knowledge, made on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: Jean-Rene Ruez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it was made on the 12th of July, for the reason that this is the only day where Serb press personnel was present in Potocari, and this is also the day when General Mladic gave a press interview. So I do believe that this interview was given on July 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. Harmon, do you have any additional questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I have just one question, Mr. Ruez, which you may be able to answer. If you can't, perhaps it's in the domain of the later witnesses. But I gather from your testimony and the exhibits that were attached thereto that virtually, if not entirely, all of these movements from the primary grave sites to the secondary grave sites took place within a period of several weeks in September and very early October. Is that approximately right?

utterances.speaker: Jean-Rene Ruez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Obviously holes were pre-dug, and later on, probably in one night or two night's operation, these holes were then filled with the bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Are you in a position to tell us in an enterprise of that magnitude the numbers, which we'll go into later, that were moved from one site to another, how much -- for instance, take any one of the grave sites where it was moved from a primary site to a secondary site. How long, approximately -- would that be; a couple of day's work or just a couple of hours' work? How much time and effort, trucks, et cetera, would it have taken to make one of those moves?

utterances.speaker: Jean-Rene Ruez [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, indeed, believe this might be covered later on by another witness, but it took certainly at least two nights, two full nights to conduct such an operation. This is probably a minimum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Would it have taken, in your view, if you feel competent to answer, take any one of the grave sites, would it have taken just one truck or several trucks to make that kind of a move?

utterances.speaker: Jean-Rene Ruez [Resumed]
utterances.text: For each site --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Jean-Rene Ruez [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- most certainly several trucks were involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. The last part of this question: Give me a notion of the distances between the primary and the secondary sites. Take any one where a primary site was disturbed and the bodies and parts of the bodies moved to a secondary site. Was that just a matter in terms of miles or metres? How long was the distance between them?

utterances.speaker: Jean-Rene Ruez [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to anticipate on information which will be provided to you by my colleague, Dean Manning, who will explain to you the connections between primary sites and the secondary sites. So to give you these distances, I would need first to expose to you what are the links between these sites. What I can tell you now is that the longest distance which was covered was from Branjevo Farm to Cancari, and this would be -- it's a rough estimate, I'm making it currently by looking at the map, and I would say 40 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Wald. Mr. Ruez, you mentioned on several occasions during your testimony the words "remote places," that was the term you used, and often you mentioned the configuration of the terrain. I think that I already have the answer I need, but, nevertheless, I'd like to hear it from you. What is the importance and significance of this factor, this element, that is to say, the configuration of the terrain, remote places, and so forth?

utterances.speaker: Jean-Rene Ruez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said remote places. I could also have said isolated places, and even desolated places, completely destroyed places. The reason why, I believe, this is very important is that this is part of an operation aimed to conceal the crime, and this massive effort of hiding these bodies was certainly much more successful if the bodies were taken in areas where probably no one would have at least resettled for years. At the moment it was done, there was probably an expectation that no one would resettle in these places before a couple of years, and this is, indeed, what happened. The first refugees are coming back in this place, in fact, since last year, and mainly this year. So there was very little risk for the perpetrators to have someone coming across one of these sites, even by accident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell us what the reasons were? Were there any factors or reasons which led to this operation?

utterances.speaker: Jean-Rene Ruez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for sure there are some factors. I cannot say that these factors are part of the investigation. We have no ability to enter the mind of those who live it, but one has to remember the context at that time. The shuttle diplomacy was going on conducted by Mr. Richard Holbrooke who was going to Belgrade to meet Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Milosevic was in easy contact with General Mladic at that time, and I may have a wrong recollection of the date, but when I read the book of Mr. Holbrooke, I noticed that, I think, that around 10th of September 1995, he requested Mr. Milosevic, President Milosevic, to have access to the area, to give access to the area, to John Shattuck who was, at that time, under secretary of state for human rights, and John Shattuck was supposed to have the freedom of access to the area to crime scenes and mass graves. So this could be a reason why this has sped up the process of disturbing these sites, but it is also clear that at one point, the perpetrators took more time because they realised that these kinds visits would not happen so soon and, indeed, the first visit was made in January of 1996. But this is an assumption. There is no certainty at all behind it, but there might be other reasons that we are absolutely unaware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You used the term "acceleration". Can you tell us how much time, how long did this operation take all in all?

utterances.speaker: Jean-Rene Ruez [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I look at the little survey I just made of these dates, one can see that between the 7th of September and the 2nd of October, open pits are created. So it is already at some point between these dates, for sure the 27 September pits were already open. It is only later that these pits were filled and the latest pit to be closed is between the 20 October and the 23 October. So we can consider that all this period of time was used to prepare and conduct this operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And another question for you, Mr. Ruez. In this period of time, is it possible to have the basic ideas of the procedure conducted, that is to say, you said that the trenches were dug, and then the bodies were transported and placed in those trenches. So can you give us an idea of the procedure actually involved and what the steps that were taken were, in general terms.

utterances.speaker: Jean-Rene Ruez [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with these types of military activities and there will be a General coming and exposing his views about what and logistics and command efforts such an operation would take; so I'm not sure I am the relevant person to explain the methodology the army would use in such a circumstance if they were the one doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I do apologise, Mr. Ruez, it's my fault. I was speaking about procedure of displacing bodies from one location to another, the procedure of that. The organisation of how the bodies were transported; that side of the operation was what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: Jean-Rene Ruez [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this point, we have elements that we are not in a position to disclose at this point, but we have quite precise information about movements of personnel in the days before the executions took place. So I'm a bit embarrassed to already enter that field, and I turn to the Prosecutor for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We intend to present, Mr. President, more detailed information that will answer your question at a later time. If that's acceptable to the Court, I would ask Mr. Ruez defer his answer until we present that evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we're going to wait for an answer in -- during the proceedings. Mr. Ruez, as we have no further questions, we should like to express our gratitude for having come here. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, what are you going to propose next?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have an additional witness, Mr. Dean Manning, who is an investigator with the Office of the Prosecutor. And Mr. Manning's testimony will be connected, in part, to the testimony of Mr. Ruez who has described the movement, but now Mr. Manning's testimony will be more focussed and more precise. He will testify today in a summary form, about the findings of experts who conducted examinations of various grave sites from 1996, 1998 and 1999 and he will introduce for Your Honours proofs linking the primary sites to the secondary sites. If I could call Mr. Manning as my next witness, we can commence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in this testimony, Mr. President, it would be -- we have a large number of exhibits and if they could be distributed now to the parties and to Your Honours, then we will be in a position to proceed quite expeditiously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Yes, very well, Mr. Harmon, I'm in full agreement. We should, indeed, always do everything to facilitate matters and to speed up the process. Mr. Manning good morning to you. Can you hear me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are now going to read the solemn declaration that you have before you. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You may be seated. I think that you know the procedure. You're going to answer questions put to you by Mr. Harmon to begin with. Mr. Harmon, the floor is yours. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Manning.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you spell your last name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: My last name is Manning, M-a-n-n-i-n-g.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How old are you?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I'm 37 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you inform the Trial Chamber of your professional background, please.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I've been a member of the Australian Federal Police, based in Canberra, Australia, since 1993, and the majority of that time was spent in the general criminal investigations branch as a detective. I joined the OTP in August of 1998 and since that time I've been working with Team 6 in the Srebrenica investigation, specifically or mainly involved in exhumation and the coordination of all evidence from that exhumation project.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me put aside exhumations aside for just a moment. Did you and did the investigative team investigate and examine evidence found at killing sites, killing sites that did not also include mass grave sites?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you identify those principal killing sites.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Two major sites of execution which were not mass graves were the Pilica Dom in the town of Pilica and the Kravica warehouse. There was also a third site examined by myself and other team members near the sites of the Nova Kasaba mass graves. That site was known as the Svilile meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Manning, can you tell the Trial Chamber when exhumations were conducted in respect of the investigation of Srebrenica. What years?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Exhumations commenced in 1996; four sites were exhumed during that year. In 1997 there were no Srebrenica-related exhumations. In 1998 there were a further eight sites exhumed. In 1999, five sites were exhumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Have you been present during some or all of these exhumations?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I've been present at four complete exhumations, I've also visited the sites of the other exhumations after they have concluded, and I've also been present at the mortuary when the remains were examined and the artifacts also examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in conducting exhumations, did the Office of the Prosecutor hire or retain experts in various fields?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you just generally inform the Trial Chamber of the types of experts that are retained to conduct an investigation in an exhumation site.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Generally there is a chief archaeologist and sometimes a chief anthropologist to perform the same duties. The rest of the team is made up of qualified archaeologists, anthropologists, pathologists. Also a number of those people have qualifications in other aspects of archaeology such as surveying, photography. There are also police officers, either serving or retired, who, if you like, coordinate the handling of exhibits, the tagging of such, and the initial examination of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do the police officers essentially ensure that there is a proper chain of custody on evidence recovered from the grave sites?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, they ensure the evidence is photographed, logged, tagged, sealed, and the continuity of that item retained until it goes to the mortuary, and then ultimately to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now at the end of an exhumation, in a particular year, do the experts who participated in the exhumation process prepare reports?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. Specifically, the chief of the exhumation project prepares a report in relation to the exhumations under his control. That was done by Dr. William Hagland for 1996, professor Richard Wright for 1998, Professor Wright for 1999, and also Mr. Jose Baraybar for the remainder of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt this examination just to remind you, and to remind myself as well, that because we speak the same language we have to pause between question and answer because the interpreters are going to be working very, very hard and they are going to be working harder if they need to -- if we talk too fast.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So if I ask a question, if you would pause --

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- and I'll pause after I ask my next question, after your answer. Now, Mr. Manning, you've described the general type of experts that are conducting the exhumations at the sites. But in addition to those experts, did the Office of the Prosecutor engage experts to examine evidence and material that were found at those particular sites?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They contracted chief pathologists and also other experts in the United Kingdom and in the Netherlands and the United States to examine items.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For example, were ballistics experts retained to examine ballistics -- I'm sorry, shell casings that were found at the various sites?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. The United States Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms conducted examinations of shell cases from those sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were experts in the field of geology and soil analysis retained by the Office of the Prosecutor to compare soil samples between the primary grave site and the secondary sites? And if you just pause before you -- to give the interpreters time to translate the question.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct. Dr. Tony Brown from the University of Exeter in the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the Office of the Prosecutor retain experts to analyse, for example, blindfold material that were found in the primary sites and the secondary sites?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. Officers from the Netherlands Institute of Forensic Studies -- Forensic Science examined cloth blindfolds and cloth ligatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, at two of the principal killing sites, the Kravica warehouse, and the Pilica Dom, blood and tissue samples were gathered and collected and turned over to the Office of the Prosecutor. Did the Office of the Prosecutor retain experts to analyse those samples to determine if there was human DNA present in them?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. Again the Netherlands Forensic Institute provided experts to study those items.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the Office of the Prosecutor retain experts to examine the explosives residue samples that were collected from the Pilica Dom and from the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. Again, the Netherlands Forensic Institute provided experts to examine the explosives for residues.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Manning, are the expert reports that had been prepared in 1996, 1998, and 1999 voluminous reports?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, they are. There's approximately 17 reports, some with multiple volumes, thousands of pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For purposes of this trial, Mr. Manning, did I ask you to prepare a summary report relating to the significant findings and conclusions of the experts from the analyses of grave sites and crime scenes in 1996, 1998, and 1999?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did I also ask you to incorporate into your report the findings of the various experts who analysed the physical evidence that was retrieved from those various sites?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you prepare a summary report that I had requested?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, can you identify for the Trial Chamber the names of the experts and the reports which are summarised in your summary report, please.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I can. There was a report from the Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms Bureau in the United States. There was a report on anthropological aspects of the 1998 bodies from Mr. Baraybar. Also a report by him in relation to the anthropological examination of human remains in 1999. Also a report by him on the exhumation of mass graves in eastern Bosnia, August to October 1999. A report by Dr. Anthony Brown in relation to soil relating to 1998 exhumations. A report by the same doctor in relation to soil analysis from 1999 exhumations. A report by Dr. John Clark on the pathology for the 1999 exhumations. A report on blood and tissue by the Dutch lab, the National Forensic Institute by Dr. A.D. Klosterman. The same lab, the examination of blindfolds and their relationships from one site to another, by Ms. Suzie Maljaars. And that same laboratory, the forensic examination of explosive residues from various sites. There's also five volumes of a report on the forensic investigation of the Cerska grave site by Dr. William Hagland. Five volumes of a report by Dr. Hagland in relation to the Lazete 2 grave site, which is also known as Orahovac. A report by Dr. Hagland in relation to four graves in the area of Nova Kasaba. A report by Dr. Hagland, four volumes, in relation to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the witness could speak up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Also if one of the microphones could be turned on. It appears that one of the microphones is not on.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: As I said, a report from Dr. Hagland in relation to the Branjevo Military Farm or Pilica mass grave site, four volumes. Eight reports from Dr. Chris Lawrence relating to autopsies of the 1998 graves. Four volumes of the United States Naval Investigations examination of the Pilica Dom and Kravica warehouse. A report by Professor Richard Wright in relation to the 1998 exhumations, eight sites. And a report by Professor Richard Wright in relation to the 1999 exhumations at Kozluk.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Manning, I don't intend to ask you detailed questions about the contents of each of those reports because we're going to be hearing from Dr. Hagland and we're going to be hearing from Dr. Lawrence and we're going to be hearing from many of those experts. The purpose of your testimony is to essentially inform the Judges of the general findings of these -- many of these experts and the connections between the primary grave sites and the secondary grave sites. For purposes of your testimony, I know you're going to be using the terms "primary grave site" and "secondary grave site". Can you define those terms as you intend to use them.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Put simply, the primary graves that I refer to are graves in which the persons or victims were placed immediately after or at the time of their execution and buried within those graves. A secondary grave is one in which the bodies are placed after they've been removed from the primary grave or, as I refer to it, "robbed" from the primary graves and placed into secondary graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Manning, what's the total number of grave sites associated with Srebrenica that have been completely exhumed and where the mortal remains of humans have been found?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: There have been 17 complete exhumations since 1996. In all those cases, multiple remains have been found.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before we take your report, let me ask you to identify the report that you prepared, and it is Prosecutor's Exhibit 140. Can you identify the title of your report, please?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes that report is entitled, "United Nations International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia Srebrenica Investigation Summary of Forensic Evidence-Execution Points and Mass Graves". It's marked as OTP 140.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, will you take Exhibit 140 and place on the ELMO page number 4/21. We need to see the whole page in the -- can you lower that a little, please. A little bit lower, please, Mr. Usher. That's fine, thank you. Mr. Manning, would you, using the pointer, explain what this is to the Court and to the people in the gallery.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a representation of the number of graves that we have exhumed and haven't exhumed to date. In this column, we have the exhumed graves, and in this column we have the graves that we have not yet exhumed. In 1996, we exhumed the Cerska grave, the Nova Kasaba grave which I refer to as "96" as we exhumed a grave in a similar area in 1999. There is a grave at Orahovac which is known as Lazete 2, a grave at Branjevo Military Farm which is also known as Pilica. Those exhumations were conducted by Dr. Hagland. In 1998, the site known as the dam near Petkovci was exhumed as was Cancari Road 12, Cancari Road 3, Hodzici Road 3, Hodzici Road 4, Hodzici Road 5, a site known as Lipje 2 and a site known as Zeleni Jadar 5. Those graves were exhumed by Professor Wright with the exception of the dam site. The remainders are secondary graves with the dam sites being a robbed primary grave. During 1999, Professor Wright conducted the exhumations of the grave at Kozluk, and Mr. Baraybar then in 1999 as the Nova Kasaba which I've indicated as the 1999 Nova Kasaba grave, a few kilometres from the 1996 site, also a site at Konjevic Polje 1 and Konjevic Polje 2, and a site known as Glogova 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, while we're on this particular chart, some of the names appear to be shaded and some are unshaded. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The names of the graves that are shaded indicate primary graves. In this case, Cerska is a primary grave that was not tampered with or robbed; Nova Kasaba was 96, was not tampered or robbed; Orahovac Lazete was; Branjevo Military Farm was; the dam at Petkovci was disturbed. The grave at Kozluk was disturbed. The grave at Nova Kasaba was not. Konjevic Polje 1 was not. Konjevic Polje 2 was not and Glogova was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So the shading in on page 4/21 are primary graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Primary graves, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The unshaded are secondary graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The unshaded graves are secondary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in the column on the right, "examined but not exhumed", what do you mean by "examined"?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The graves in the white column indicate graves in which we have either by mechanically digging or trenching, established that there are human remains, multiple human remains within those graves. We have not yet been able to exhume them. Again the grey shading on Lazete 1 or Orahovac and on Glogova 1 indicate that they are primary graves. The remainder of the graves are secondary graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me turn your attention, Mr. Manning, to another exhibit that's on the easel. It's Prosecutor's Exhibit 135. Your Honours should have an A-3 size of Prosecutor's Exhibit 135. Let me turn your attention to this large exhibit and can you explain, first of all, using this exhibit, the location of the primary grave sites using the -- there's a pointer. Perhaps you can approach. There is a microphone. Will you just identify the primary mass grave sites? First indicating the ones that were disturbed?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Firstly, the Branjevo Military Farm at the top of the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why don't you take the microphone from the usher, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This grave is a primary grave which was disturbed in that bodies were taken from that grave. This is the grave at Kozluk next to the Drina River. Again, a primary grave that was disturbed. This is the Petkovci dam or the dam near Petkovci site. Again, that was disturbed. This is the two sites at Orahovac, also known as Lazete. Lazete 2 was disturbed. We have not yet exhumed Lazete 1. In the south, we have the site known as Glogova. Primary graves, Glogova 2 has been exhumed and was a disturbed grave, Glogova one has not been exhumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, using the pointer, show the Court on this exhibit the undisturbed primary grave sites.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The undisturbed primary grave sites are clustered in this area of the map. They include Cerska, a primary grave, Nova Kasaba, Nova Kasaba 1999, a grave known as Konjevic Polje 1, and Konjevic Polje 2. All primary and all undisturbed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. Have a seat. Now, Mr. Manning, if you would kindly take Prosecutor's Exhibit 140, your report, and turn to the page which has the numbers 00950925, and place that on the ELMO, please. Can you briefly explain what this particular chart is that you prepared?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This chart shows the primary graves in relation to the Srebrenica investigation. Graves here in red, are the undisturbed primary graves, the ones that I indicated on the map in one particular area. Graves here in blue indicate primary graves which have been disturbed or robbed of some of the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Manning, I'm not going to ask you to approach the board again because we had extensive testimony from Mr. Ruez identifying the secondary mass grave sites, but on Prosecutor 135, do the green dots on that exhibit represent the locations of the second mass grave sites?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, they do. They represent the collection of secondary graves that we're aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if you turn to the next page in Prosecutor's Exhibit 140 which is found at 00950926, would you place that on the ELMO, please, and this is a summary chart and it has certain information. Can you explain to the Judges what this chart contains?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: In a similar fashion to the previous chart, it shows the secondary mass graves. All the graves listed are ones in which we are aware that multiple human remains have been found. The graves that are indicated by the dark green filled-in areas, are the graves that we've exhumed during the past few years. These other graves are graves that we have not yet exhumed but, again, they contain multiple human remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: They've been probed?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Been probed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me correct this chart. In the top of the middle column below it, it says "Hodzici Road 2" and "Hodzici Road 2". Can we correct the top box?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: It should read "Hodzici Road 1".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Manning. Now, we had extensive general discussion about the robbing of these graves, and since you participated in the exhumations and had frequent contacts with the experts. When an exhumation at a particular site was being conducted, could it be determined from examining the soil and examining the texture of the soil and the composition of the soil whether or not particular grave site had been tampered with? And you can answer that yes or no because I'm going to show you some exhibits and I'll ask you to explain it in a minute.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if I could have Prosecutor's Exhibit -- it's a large exhibit, 135 -- I'm sorry, it is 1J1 placed on the easel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, you're familiar with this exhibit and while it's being placed on the easel, does Prosecutor's Exhibit 1J1 show any evidence of a disturbance at a primary mass grave site?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please feel free to approach the exhibit on the easel and, using the pointer, will you explain to the Judges the significance of this particular photograph.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a photograph of the Kozluk mass grave site that was exhumed in 1999. This represents bodies on the surface of the soil which I'm told was the original surface, the original level. As you can see, this group of bodies here appears to have been cut through, it's at the bottom middle of the page, by this trench that runs through this section of the photograph. As that section of the trench cuts through the original surface, it must have been made after this surface had the bodies on it. Therefore, this trench here cut through the grave and removed at least parts of these bodies here and some of the soil.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. The soil then from this particular site and the bodies that were -- and the parts of the bodies that were taken from that site were transported to a secondary site and I take it, Mr. Manning, that the soil that was take taken from this trench was then the basis of a later comparison by experts to determine whether the soil found in the secondary grave had come, for example, from this grave.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now you can have a seat, Mr. Manning, please, and I'm going to ask the usher to assist you in placing an exhibit on the ELMO. It's Prosecutor's Exhibit 132/107. Do you have a copy of that exhibit with you?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, that's a copy of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this is Prosecutor's Exhibit 132/107, and let me ask, has that been distributed to the parties? It should be in Your Honours' -- Your Honours should have some binders and it should be in the binder marked "132." There will be a tab in your binder that's before Your Honours that says "107."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Manning, where is this site?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The site depicted on this exhibit is the same as the large exhibit on the easel. It's the Kozluk primary mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you speak up, please.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: It's the Kozluk primary mass grave, as in the larger exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, what does this particular exhibit illustrate that is not illustrated in the previous exhibit?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: It's, in effect, the same photograph. As you can see, this line through the middle of the page is the cutout shown on the large picture. It shows the more extensive trenching or cutting of the base of that area and it shows the extension through this area, to the right of the picture, where soil and bodies have been removed from that grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Does this give any clue as to what kind of a device was used to remove the bodies? And if so, can you explain.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. I've been informed by the chief archaeologists that this would represent a mechanical digger or trenching machine such as a -- similar to a bulldozer with a bucket that could scoop into the soil and make these sort of marks. It also leaves wheel marks on the base of the soil.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, can you inform the Trial Chamber the effect of this removal process on the bodies in the primary grave and the evidence that is associated with those bodies.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: It's difficult not to overstate the effect that removing of the bodies has had on the investigation. As you can see in this exhibit, the bodies appear to be cut through. You can see that a large amount of soil and bodies have been removed. They were removed by a bucketed machine, in effect, scooped up, placed in the back of a truck or dumped in the back of a truck, which would mean the body parts would be further broken up, and driven some distance over rough roads before being placed in a secondary grave in a similar manner, or dumped. That will cause the body and body parts to break apart, to mix up, to fall in different areas, effectively spreading the bodies across both sites and across the sites. It has meant that identification of the individuals has become extremely difficult, it has meant that items which would lead to identification have been damaged and destroyed, and instead of exhuming the primary graves within a year or two we are at the stage where we've only be able to exhume a part of the graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Mr. Manning. Now I'd like to focus your attention on the general findings of these experts, and if you would refer to page 3/21 of Prosecutor's Exhibit 140, your report. I'd like to start out with just some statistics, your providing some statistics, please, and the reason I ask you to just provide the statistics is we're going to be hearing from the experts themselves shortly. But can you first of all tell the Court the minimum number of individuals who were located at all of the exhumed sites. How many are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The MNI, or minimal number of individuals, is 1,883.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you define the term "minimal number of individuals"?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: It's a complicated term that will obviously be explained at greater length by the experts. But as the bodies have been broken up in the robbing process, it's not simply a matter of counting the bodies, which would be the case with an undisturbed grave such as Cerska. With the disturbed primary grave and secondary grave, the bodies are so intermingled that a simple count won't work. They're damaged. Anthropologists calculate the minimum number of individuals by selecting normally a large bone and a left or right bone and only counting that bone, in effect, a thigh bone, all left thigh bones. From that they calculate the minimum number of people that would be represented by those bones. If those bones aren't present or are damaged, then they can't be counted. It then gets more complicated. Basically it's a count of a selected large bone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, the use of the minimum number of individuals and the formula that you've described, is that a conservative approach to numbering the victims?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Very conservative. If that particular bone is not present or damaged, then it's not counted. You could have an entire body minus a leg or part of a leg and it would be difficult to count that body. So it is a very conservative number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Does that lead to the likelihood that in the 22 fully exhumed grave sites there are more than 1,883 individuals in those sites?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: In the 17 exhumed --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Seventeen, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. There would be, I believe, more than that, and in fact there are large numbers of body parts in some graves which certainly outnumber the number of whole bodies. I would expect that number to be greater.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, does the figure 1,883, the minimum number of individuals, include the number of individuals found in the probed sites?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: No, it does not. They have not been counted in that 1,883.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, please turn your attention to the gender of the victims found in the various exhumed sites. Can you provide the Trial Chamber with the statistics in that regard, please.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: In relation to the assessment of sex of the victims, 1,656 individuals were determined to be male; 212 individuals were undetermined, that is, no sex was determined for them; 1 individual was determined to be a female.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention now to the statistics in respect of the cause of death. Would you please summarise the findings.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: As to cause of death, 1,424 individuals died as a result of gunshot wounds; 169 individuals died of probable or possible gunshot wounds; 5 individuals died of shrapnel injuries; 4 died of other causes, such as trauma or possible suffocation; and 1,374 individuals died of undetermined causes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now if I could have placed on the easel Prosecutor's Exhibit 1/H/I, we're going to turn our attention to the blindfolds because they play an important part in this case and in linking the various sites. Let me ask you first, Mr. Manning, did the people conducting the exhumations discover the presence of blindfolds in various mass grave sites?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this is an image. Can you first of all identify this image and what it shows.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This image is a victim from the Kozluk mass grave. This is during the exhumation process. This photo depicts the individual with a cloth blindfold over his eyes. It also shows his arms bent backwards behind him in the area of the belt, and some of the vegetation and other artefacts in the grave, including near his head, the boot of another victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: My apologies. That individual was also bound at the wrists.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me show you an exhibit which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 149. It's an A4-size photograph. If that could be placed on the easel, please. Can you identify this particular photograph, Mr. Manning.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again this photo is from the Kozluk mass grave. It was during the 1999 exhumation. This photograph shows one of the archaeologists in the process of exhuming this body. As you can see on the right-hand middle side of the image, there's the head and part of the body of the victim, with the mouth. Across the eyes is a cloth blindfold, tied at the back of the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Manning, in the course of the exhumation work photographs are made of the various bodies and then the items that are found on these bodies, such as the blindfolds and other items, are identified, preserved, and retained by the Office of the Prosecutor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, could I have Prosecutor's Exhibit 27/9, which is a physical exhibit, shown to the witness; 27/9 is the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, do you have in front of you an example of one of the blindfolds that was retrieved from the Kozluk site? Could you remove it, please, and show the Court.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I have it in front of me. Excuse me. I'll just place some gloves on. This artefact is marked "KK-3" for Kozluk, grave 3, "834B," for body 834, and also marked as "A1." It's a cloth with a knot at the back of it, and a metal tag identifying it. It also has what I believe to be hair and human tissue adhering to it. As you can see, it was spread out and has since shrunk a little bit in the washing process. But it's the blindfold that you see on that image on the large easel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So it's the blindfold on the man who is depicted in the large image on the easel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's the blindfold removed from that body.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's this kind of material that then was submitted for expert analysis for comparison purposes with other blindfolds that are found at secondary sites; is that right? This kind of material, blindfold material.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This sort of material and cloth of this type that was also used as a ligature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if I could have Prosecutor's Exhibit -- actually let me ask you another question first, Mr. Manning. How many different exhumation sites were blindfolds and cloth material discovered?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: From eight separate sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, can you identify those sites orally, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For purposes of assisting Your Honours, at page 21/21 in Mr. Manning's report, there is a table that will provide the Chamber with statistics about blindfolds, their locations where they were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, can you just identify orally the locations of those sites, please.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, the sites were the Branjevo Military Farm, which is a primary grave. The related secondary grave of Cancari Road 12, the primary grave at Orahovac known as Lazete 2, the three connected secondary graves at Hodzici Road 3, Hodzici Road 4 and Hodzici Road 5. Also at the Kozluk site, as you've seen, and the Cancari Road 3 site which is the associated secondary for that grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have Prosecutor's Exhibit 130/96 placed on the ELMO, please. THE REGISTRAR [Interpretation] Your Honours, it can be found in the binders.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Sorry Mr. Harmon, can you tell me that exhibit number again?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is a blindfold that was taken from Orahovac and it appears to be coloured material; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This also provided indications to the people who were doing the expert analysis when they would find something of this colour, they would compare it to a similar coloured material from a different site in attempting to reach their conclusions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Remove that, please, from the ELMO. Now, could I have placed on the easel Prosecutor's Exhibit 142, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, how many blindfolds were discovered at the various sites that were exhumed?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: In total, at least 270 blindfolds were found at those eight sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is that a conservative figure?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Some blindfolds had deteriorated to the point that we couldn't use them. Some had been dislodged. This is a conservative figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you explain now -- there's a board on the easel with many, many small photographs. Can you explain to the Judges what that represents. The Judges have also been provided with an A-3 sized copy of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This represents a photo of each of the blindfolds located. It -- there were one or two photos that showed two blindfolds but effectively, this is the 270 blindfolds located within those graves. They are in order of grave. The first section is the grave designation. Some of those blindfolds are in situ on the head, others are photographed at the morgue after cleaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, Prosecutor's Exhibit 128, 129 and 130 are the binders with individual photographs that are depicted on this collective, this collage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you tell the Judges how you made this selection of these images, please, what methodology you used, why you were conservative in your approach and how you were conservative in your approach?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I examined all the records, photographs, expert reports in relation to the discovery of blindfolds. But as you can see from some of the photographs, they are difficult to see. They are difficult to see due to the condition of the bodies. They would have been logged at the exhumation side; however, some of those blindfolds would move or slip or be dislodged on transportation to the morgue, and the morgue will also find blindfolds loose on the body and part of the associated artefacts. Therefore the count of blindfolds from the exhumation site and from the morgue would be different. I examined those counts. I physically examined the blindfolds, and I selected only those blindfolds that were either mentioned by the archaeologist, mentioned by the pathologist, anthropologist, photographed in situ or were clearly a blindfold due to their construction material, and normally the presence of human hair in the knot or pieces of what appeared to be scalp and skull on those pieces of cloth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know what time you would like to take a break but if you -- I can very easily continue this examination, but if I know, then I can orient myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is indeed a good time because we've been working for an hour and 15 minutes. Let us now have a 20-minute break and we can continue after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Maybe before we take the break, I can introduce the exhibits that were tendered by Mr. Ruez. We had not formally tendered those exhibits and I can identify those for Your Honours. It would be 28/7, 28/9, 28/11, 28/18, 28/8, and then 160 through 169, and 184 through 187.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, have you any objections to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence does not have any objections to the exhibits presented by the Prosecution; however, the Defence does have a proposal, that is, to officially tender D20, Exhibit D20 during the testimony of Witness T.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well. Mr. Harmon, any objections with respect to D20 and its tendering?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me have one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it ought to be under seal, an exhibit under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but we have had that observation by Mr. Petrusic, and as it is a protected witness, the declaration must be under seal, admitted under seal. The exhibits, Prosecution, as they were numbered, 7, 9, 11, 18, 8, 169, 184 through 187, and Exhibits D20 have been tendered and admitted. Very well. Let us now have a 20-minute break after which we shall continue the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, before we start your testimony, let me ask you to keep your voice up. We're going to change the topic now. We're going to turn to the topic of ligatures. Let me ask you, during the course of the exhumation process, was it determined that some of the victims, or many of the victims had had their hands or their arms tied with ligatures of various types of material?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, during the recess I placed Prosecutor's Exhibit 141 on the easel; it's a collage. The Judges should have an A3-size copy of Prosecutor's Exhibit 141 in front of them for their own reference. Let me ask you, Mr. Manning, can you explain what's depicted in this particular exhibit.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, this exhibit is similar to the blindfold collage. It shows the ligatures that were located at the various graves. The grave name is indicated in the first white section and continues to show all the ligatures that I could identify from those graves. A total of 407 ligatures of different types.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, Prosecutor's Exhibits 128, 129, 130, and 131 have the individual images that are contained in the collage, so for your later reference the sum individual parts of this exhibit are found in those binders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Manning, once again let me ask you, the figure of 407 ligatures that are depicted in the exhibits, is this a conservative number?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, it's conservative.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For the same reasons that you gave in respect of the blindfold material?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Exactly the same reason, and indeed some of the ligatures were cloth which deteriorated; some were wire which broke apart. Exactly the same methodology was applied to the ligatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, referring to page 20/21 of your summary report, can you identify the sites, the exhumation sites, where these ligatures were found, and can you make a distinction in making these identifications between a primary site and a secondary site.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. Ligatures were found at Cerska grave. This is a primary grave. Almost all those ligatures were of wire. The Nova Kasaba primary grave of 1996, ligatures were also found. Both those graves were not disturbed. At the Orahovac (Lazete 2) grave, a ligature was found; that is a primary grave, and at the related secondary grave of Hodzici Road 5, a ligature was also found. At the primary disturbed grave of Branjevo Military Farm, ligatures were found, and at the related secondary grave at Cancari Road 12. Similarly, ligatures were found at the primary site of the dam near Petkovci and its related site of Liplje 2. They were also found at the primary grave of Kozluk and its associated secondary grave of Cancari Road 3. Ligatures were also found at the secondary site of Zeleni Jadar 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did your analysis of these ligatures reveal that there were different types of ligature material used on the victims?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. Different materials were used. Some were used opportunistically, such as a cloth sack. But predominantly there were ligatures of wire, mainly two types of wire; there were ligatures of cloth; there were ligatures of string.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me start by putting on the easel Prosecutor's Exhibit 134. We're going to use a series of exhibits to illustrate the different kinds of ligature material that were found in the various exhumation sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you stand that up, Mr. Usher? That's the correct perspective.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, on the easel is Prosecutor's Exhibit 134, Mr. Manning. Can you approach that, please, using the microphone, and identify the significant parts of that exhibit, please. First of all, where is this image, taken from which grave site?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This image is from the Kozluk primary grave, mass grave site. It shows an individual who is laying on his face and front, with the head and skull up here, two arms here, the belt and rest of the body down here to the end of the photo. Clearly around the arm and wrists of this individual is a ligature made of twine or string, white synthetic twine. It is tied in a knot here and goes round both wrists of this individual. This individual also has a blindfold.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Manning. Please sit down. Mr. Manning, I'd like to now put on the ELMO Prosecutor's Exhibit 132/86, which is a cloth ligature example, please. Could you please explain this particular exhibit, where it's located -- where the photograph is taken, from which site, and what kind of material is used in this particular illustration.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This particular image is from the Branjevo Military Farm, or Pilica. It represents human remains that have been found during the exhumation process. There are a set of hands and arms. The rest of the body has not yet been exposed. You can see that the arms are crossed over in the area of the wrist, and here is a cloth ligature, again knotted and wrapping round both wrists. Some of these cloth ligatures formed a figure 8; some of them formed a circle, but all of them bound and knotted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's turn to the next exhibit, Mr. Manning, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 132/87. Would you place that on the ELMO, please, and explain to the Court what that represents. Could you turn it to the side, please.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a photograph of a ligature binding of the hands and wrists of an individual from the Nova Kasaba 1996 mass grave. You can see the victim's coat sleeve. This is one of his hands and this is another of his hands. Binding and digging into the flesh is a wire ligature, again knotted or tied around the wrists.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, can you show the Court, using Prosecutor's Exhibit 16/6, what a wire ligature that was retrieved from one of these sites looks like. You should have it in front of you. Mr. Manning, if you would remove that from the bag, please.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a wire ligature, and marked on the bag is "CSK," which is the code for Cerska, "108," which is the body that it came from, and the number 2, which indicates artefact 2. This is now in two parts. It is a wire ligature. At one stage it was passing around the wrists of the individual through one loop, and through the other loop was the other wrist. It is bound here and twisted and tied. As you can see, it is quite small. It was very tightly bound around the wrists.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Manning. Now, Mr. Manning, we'll turn to another important category of evidence which is the presence of artefacts, as I call it, at the various grave sites, and during the exhumations. Did the Office of the Prosecutor recover different types of artefacts that were significant and that led to the identification, first of all, of the victims having come from Srebrenica and, second of all, to the actual identifications of some of those victims?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct. In each of the graves that we exhumed, documentation or other items were found which provided a positive link to Srebrenica. They included licna carte or licence cards, identification, other. In some instances, they have provided identification of the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe, just in -- using a general example, how the discovery of an artefact in a mass grave site leads to the identification of someone from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: In the general sense, the licence card may have the address or the opstina of Srebrenica on it. It may be some other artefact as documentation from factories, offices, receipts naming Srebrenica or addresses in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, have artefacts linked to Srebrenica been located in all of the primary mass grave sites?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, every one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Also located in the exhumed secondary -- all of the exhumed secondary sites?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: There's been something to link the individuals to Srebrenica in all the cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What I'd like to do now, Mr. Manning is run through a series of exhibits to illustrate the types of artefacts that are discovered in these graves and we'll start with first of all Prosecutor's Exhibit 132/95. There is a related exhibit to that and that is 132/95A. But if you would put 132/95 on the ELMO first. Can you tell, first of all, where that particular artefact was retrieved?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This artefact was removed from body number 60 or human remains number 60 at the Cerska grave. "CSK" is the code for Cerska, 1996, primary grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I'll just move it down a bit. It's a pendant, a gold coloured pendant or necklace with an "S" as part of the pattern. You can also see on the top of the photo a knot in the chain of that pendant. This was removed from the victim, Cerska 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Manning, this ultimately led to an identification which we'll get to in a minute. Can you please tell the Court how this led to an identification and the story related to this particular object?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: As part of the attempt to interview, to identify the victims from Srebrenica, families would report the missing to known government organisations such as PHR and the International Red Cross. In that process, they would provide as much information as they could on the description of the individual; age, height, injuries. Also personal effects such as clothing, such as wallets, such as medallions such as this. This particular thing was identified by a family prior to it being investigated by the OTP. They drew a picture of a pendant with an S on it and a knot in the chain. On the basis of that, on the basis of the description of the individual, and the post mortem data, they established that the individual Cerska 60 was the individual that had been identified as wearing this chain and this pendant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What were the circumstances under which the victim came to wear this particular pendant? Would you tell the Judges what information the Office of the Prosecutor found out?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The pendant was given to the individual, who was a young boy, by his mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: In Srebrenica. It was given to him. She detailed that to PHR.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you describe, please, the story?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: She indicated that she gave him the chain as a gift. He placed it around his neck. Because of his small size, it was too long. She saw him knot it to make it a little bit easier to wear. She was able to identify the pendant itself, particularly the "S" and, more importantly, identify the knot that she saw her son put in that chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, how old was the boy?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: He was born in 1979 according to the identification material, so that made him 15, 16 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you place Prosecutor's Exhibit 132/95A on the ELMO. There's a name that's highlighted on that. First of all, what is this list?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a page from the list prepared by ICRC or International Red Cross and PHR. It indicates the name of the missing from Srebrenica. It's a large volume. This indicates the missing identified victim's name as Samir Spiodic, a male, his date of birth which is the 22nd of February 1979. It also indicates the place of birth, Srebrenica, his father's name, Kamel, date and place of disappearance, and it also indicates the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's turn to another example, Mr. Manning. Prosecutor's Exhibit 132/93. Can you place that on the ELMO, please. Explain what this is and what its significance is.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This item was recovered from the mass grave at Branjevo Military Farm. It's marked as Pilica, the code for that grave, 16, and item 10. It's the 10th item removed from body 16 from that grave. And as can be seen, it's an artificial leg. It was removed from that victim. Repairing or binding that leg is an amount of tape. On that tape are the words "Feros Uniz Srebrenica and Yugoslavia." On the basis of the data provided by the family, that false leg led to the identification of PLC-16.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you place Prosecutor's Exhibit 132/93A on the ELMO. Identify this object first of all and then tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, it's a page detailing persons missing from Srebrenica. This is a PHR, ICRC missing list. It provides the name of the victim, Nezir Efendic, a male, the year he was born, his father's name, and where he went missing from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's turn again to an example of an artefact that was significant and was discovered in one of the mass grave sites. Could you please put Prosecutor's Exhibit 132/91 on the ELMO. Tell us about this particular exhibit, Mr. Manning.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: If I can just move it up. This is a licence card or licna carte which was recovered from the secondary mass grave of Hodzici Road 3 which is indicated here. It's from body 3, and it's the seventh artefact from that body. There is a photograph still partly visible of a male person and the details of that individual, date of birth, father's name, his name, where he's from, Srebrenica, is included on that licence card.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, what's the date of birth that's indicated on that licna carte licence card?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: 17th of June, 1919.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you turn to the next exhibit which is related, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 132/91A. Please tell us about this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, it's a page of details of missing from Srebrenica. It includes the details of the identified person from the Hodzici Road grave, Abdurahman Avdic, male, and a year of birth and, again, date and place of birth, Srebrenica, father's name, and date and place of disappearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the year of birth is different in this exhibit, it's the year 1920, and in the previous exhibit it was 1919. Nevertheless, was there a confirmation that the individual whose licence card licna carte was found in the grave site is this?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This individual has been positively identified, that identification accepted by the Bosnian authorities, and a death certificate issued. I believe, and I've had experience with the details provided by the family. They are often wrong in the sense that they don't know the precise year of birth and, as indicated here, they can't recall or don't know the day and month of birth. I've spoken to witnesses who didn't know their own date of birth, month or even year.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning, let's turn to another exhibit, please. Prosecutor's Exhibit 132/98. Turn it on its side so we can see the whole exhibit. Mr. Manning, what does this exhibit tell us?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This exhibit is from the Cancari Road 3, the secondary grave to Kozluk. It's from body or may even represent body 372 from that grave. As you can see, it's part of a spinal column of an individual. In this case, due to medical conditions best described by experts, the spine has been fused along its length. Obviously, this individual would be unable to freely move or bend and he was subject to an autopsy report that details that condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That autopsy report that details his condition is Prosecutor's Exhibit 132/98A. You don't have to put that on the ELMO, but does that autopsy report indicate that this was a man who was disabled as a result of this condition?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: From the autopsy report, the whole spine showed a severe ancylosis which would have caused obvious problems in moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this is a unique medical condition for this particular victim. Has this led to an identification of the victim?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Not in this case, it hasn't led to an identification. Those efforts are still continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's turn to another type of artefact that was found in, I think, the exhumed sites if we could turn to Prosecutor's Exhibit 132/109. Again, Mr. Manning, please tell us where this was located and what this particular object is and what it represents.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This object was removed from the Hodzici 4 secondary grave related to the Orahovac Lazete graves. It is removed from body 296, and it's artefact 2. The other details include the photographic numbers and the date. As you can see, it is a pocket watch with what is obviously a hole or mark through it apparently caused by a bullet or similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did this artefact corroborate the medical findings on the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. The cause of death of this individual indicated gunshot wounds, multiple gunshot wounds. This being in his possession is indicative of being struck by those bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now this, for Your Honours' benefit, we won't put this on the ELMO as Prosecutor's Exhibit 132/109A. Let's turn now, Mr. Manning, to another type of evidence that confirms that people who are located in these exhumed sites were of the Muslim faith. Could you please place 132/110 on the ELMO. Now, first of all, tell us if, in the course of the exhumations, Muslim religious objects were retrieved from various sites.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: In the majority of sites, Muslim religious artefacts were located, such as small copies of the Koran, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Explain what is in Prosecutor's Exhibit 132/110, please.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This item was removed from Hodzici 3 grave. The "A" and the number indicates it's an artefact which normally means separate from a body. It was loose in the grave; during the disturbance it separated. It was a plastic packing which included this script, which is a long thin sheet of paper with apparent Muslim verses on it; I've been informed that it's of a religious nature. It's indicative of the sorts of religious texts, or Muslim texts located in the graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is an example of an artefact that confirms at least that some of the victims within the site exhumed are of Muslim faith.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Let's turn now to the next exhibit, Mr. Manning, 132/1. This is also under a different exhibit number introduced earlier, 1.G. It is a photograph, Mr. Manning. If you'd be so kind as to place that on the ELMO and tell us where it was found, and generally the significance of photographs that are found along with bodies.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is Exhibit 132/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We need to pan up so that the whole exhibit can be seen. Just down a little bit, please, Mr. Usher. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This item was removed from the Lazete or Orahovac grave. Lazete 2 is the grave designation, and body 36, and it's one of at least 12 items recovered from that body. It's obviously a family photo, a snapshot. This individual had a number of photographs in his possession, in his wallet. The photographs have allowed us, in some instances, to identify the victims. These photographs can be shown to the surviving relatives. On occasion that has proved difficult as the photographs deteriorate rather quickly. In this instance you can still see the individuals that this man carried around.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, earlier in your testimony you touched on the effect of the removal of bodies from the primary sites to the secondary sites. Is one of the consequences of essentially robbing the graves and trying to hide the mortal remains of these victims that physical evidence, such as photographs that have been hidden at different locations and therefore take a longer time to find because each grave has not yet completely been exhumed, does that result in the deterioration of physical evidence?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Very much so. This photograph was exhumed with the body in 1996 but you can still see it has deteriorated, or did then. Photographs removed from the graves in 1999 are either destroyed, or I've seen them disappear as they are exposed to air.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, let's turn to the next exhibit, please, 132/4. It's another photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We need to lower that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What is this photograph, where was it found, and has it led to an identification?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This photograph was found with Lazete 2 or Orahovac, body 36. Again it's part of item 12 so it's with that other photograph. It's a young girl, a child, in a pink dress, normal family photographs that were with this victim. In this case it hasn't led to an identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's turn to the next exhibit, please, Mr. Manning. Prosecutor's Exhibit 132/6.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please connect this exhibit to the site and tell us the significance of this exhibit, please. Turn it the other way, please. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This exhibit, again from the same grave and the same body, item 12, and it is a photo or part of a photo of a small boy. Also of interest is the tape that's binding that photograph and other photographs at the back of it. Again, it's the Feros Uniz Srebrenica, Yugoslavia-type that we saw on the artificial leg from the Branjevo Military Farm grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So these photographs and the previous two photographs have not led to identifications, but there is evidence from the tape indicating Srebrenica that these are probably from somebody from Srebrenica; is that a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, that's a fair assessment, or my assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
