utterances.text: All right. Now let's turn to the last in the series of these exhibits, 132/18. Mr. Manning, again orient us to this particular exhibit.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, a family photo. This was removed from body number 11, at Pilica, or the Branjevo Military Farm. This individual had a photograph of, we assume, his family. As a result of this and other information, that individual was identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, would you kindly take Prosecutor's Exhibit 132/18A, and you said that photograph led to an identification. Who was the victim in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The victim who carried that photograph was Elizabet Selimovic, a male; date of birth: 30th of January, 1962; again, date and place of birth, Bratunac; father's name; and date and place of disappearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Mr. Manning, on that series of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, I'm finished with that series of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What I'd like to turn your attention to now, Mr. Manning, is focus on some of the types of other evidence that led to connecting and linking the primary grave sites to the secondary grave sites. In your earlier testimony you said that the Office of the Prosecutor had retained various experts: ballistic experts, soil analysis experts, materials analysis experts, comparing cloth samples, blindfolds and ligatures, from one grave site to the other. You said that there have been comparative analyses run on these objects; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What I'd like to do, first of all, Mr. Manning, is start with the ballistics experts, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could have placed on the easel Prosecutor's Exhibit 133. That should be placed on the side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: First of all, did the Office of the Prosecutor, in the course of conducting these exhumations, recover shell casings from the primary and secondary sites?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, shell casings were recovered from all the sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, were all of the shell casings from all the sites recovered or only samples?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Only samples. There were shell casings at sites that were not collected.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, focusing your attention on Prosecutor's Exhibit 133, first of all can you identify from which site this photograph is taken.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, this is from the Kozluk mass grave site, exhumed in 1999, a primary site, primary disturbed site.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you approach the exhibit, please, using the easel, and explain to the Trial Chamber the significance of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is an exhumation photograph. They have presented or uncovered part of the body. You can see that it's an individual with his legs running through here to the bottom of the photo; skull and head with a blindfold; his arms behind his back, bound. General artefacts within the grave: Notably on this is a shell case here near what would be the individual's left arm. That is indicative of where we found shell cases either associated with the bodies, amongst the clothing, or in other parts of the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Manning. We're going to show another example. If we could place on the ELMO, Mr. Manning, 132/106. Please identify this exhibit and point out the significant features of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, this is from the Kozluk grave, designated by "KK-3." It is body or body parts 571, body 571. This is obviously an individual's arms and you can see that they're bound. The rest of the body has not been exposed yet. Again you can see the artefacts that are present within the grave. In this case, a shell case, a shell case, a shell case, and part of a shell case here still buried. Those are the sort of shell cases that were collected.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, then, were shell cases from primary sites, such as this at Kozluk, also collected at secondary sites?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were those or some of those shell casings submitted to the United States Treasury Department's Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms in an attempt to make a comparison to see if the shell casings from primary sites matched shell casings located in secondary sites?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President and Your Honours, the Office of the Prosecutor filed the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms' report with the Trial Chamber, pursuant to Rule 94 bis, on the 14th of April, 2000, and on the 28th of April, 2000, the Defence informed the Trial Chamber that it had accepted the statement of this expert. So we would now have and tender to the Court Prosecutor's Exhibit 144, which is the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms' ballistics report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, have you had a chance to review that report?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you first of all briefly describe to the Trial Chamber the types of analyses that were conducted by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Simply put, the shell cases collected have various marks on them caused by the firing and ejection process from the weapon. Specifically, ejector marks on shell cases, marks that were put there when the shell was ejected from the weapon after firing, were

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: microscopic examination and comparison. They would examine a shell case ejector mark on one or more shell casings and attempt to match those marks to show that that shell case had been fired by the same weapon.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Now, as a result of that analysis, were shell casings that were found in primary execution sites and grave sites matched with shell casings found in secondary mass grave sites?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Manning, would you kindly place page 14/21 from your report on the ELMO. Once it's centred, properly, Mr. Manning, I'd like you to explain the findings of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms, the location of shells from primary sites or other locations and where they matched shell casings at other locations.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: On the basis of the matches and the numbers provided by ATF, they produced this table which indicates that a shell case or shell cases from the Kravica warehouse execution point were matched by ATF to the secondary grave of Zeleni Jadar 5; that is, a shell case from Kravica and a shell case from Zeleni Jadar 5 were apparently fired by the same weapon. In the Cerska primary grave, in the grave itself, shell cases were matched to the surface of the grave, at the roadway near the grave, and the roadway on the north side of the road. In the primary grave of Orahovac, or Lazete as it's indicated here, shell cases from these areas, including the grave and the grave surface, were matched to shell cases found in the related secondary grave of Hodzici Road 3, 5, and 4. Again, the primary grave of Petkovci, the Dam near Petkovci, the shell cases on the surface of the dam matched those found within the hole, or the grave itself. The Kozluk primary mass grave surface, the shell cases match that found at the secondary site of Cancari Road 3.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Let's turn to another link connecting primary graves to secondary graves now, Mr. Manning, and that is the results of soil and pollen sample analysis. Now, in respect of primary and secondary sites that were exhumed by the Office of the Prosecutor, did the Office of the Prosecutor collect soil samples from particular primary sites and secondary sites, and did they retain those soil samples for later analysis?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Why were the soil samples from the primary sites and the secondary sites collected?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: They were collected either by Dr. Tony Brown, or at his request, in an attempt to identify the types of soil and properties of the soil that were found in one grave which were apparently picked up and transported and placed inside the secondary grave, that soil being foreign to that area; so an attempt to match the soil from the primary site to where it was dumped, if you like, in the secondary site.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: What primary and secondary sites were soil samples collected?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Soil samples were collected from the Branjevo Military Farm, from its associated secondary grave of Cancari Road 12; from the Kozluk primary grave and its associated secondary grave of Cancari Road 3; from the Orahovac Lazete site and it's associated sites of Hodzici 3, 4 and 5, and also from the primary grave of Glogova and the secondary grave of Zeleni Jadar 5.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: You said these soil samples were submitted to a Dr. Brown, can you identify him further and what his background qualifications are?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Dr. Brown is a palynologist at the University of Exeter in the UK. He has degrees in geology and he also is an expert on the identification of soil, soil types, and the artefacts found in soil such as macrofossils but more particularly pollen which represents where the soil came into contact with vegetation, specifying the area where that soil was.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Did Dr. Brown prepare an expert report and did he submit that to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: He prepared two expert reports, and he submitted them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, Dr. Brown's report for the 1998 exhumations was filed by the Prosecutor with the Trial Chamber pursuant to Rule 94 bis on January 6, 2000 and his report for the 1999 exhumations was filed by the Prosecutor's office on February 7th, 2000. On the 25th of February 2000, the Defence informed the Trial Chamber in writing pursuant to Rule 94 bis (B) that they accepted the statements of Dr. Brown. So we could tender Dr. Brown's two expert reports, Exhibit 179 which is Dr. Brown's analysis for the 1998 analysis, exhumations, I'm sorry, and Exhibit 180 which is Dr. Brown's analysis for the 1999 exhumations.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, excuse me, I think that you mentioned, quite rightly, the two reports of Anthony Brown, and it is true that the Defence has accepted the first tendered on the 6th of January, but I think that the Chamber still has no response to this day regarding Anthony Brown's report filed on the 7th of February. I don't know whether that one response applies to both reports or if the Defence has given a positive response to the first and has still not provided a response to the second. Perhaps we need to clear that up with the Defence. Mr. Petrusic, I don't know whether we are right or not, but we have not found any response in relation to the report of the 7th of February. We do have a response on the report dated the 6th of January. Can you help us, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has accepted both reports by expert Brown. I will check later if there is some technical errors, but it is our intention to accept both reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So we have your response dated the 3rd of March, 2000. But if you say that you accept both, they are accepted. No problem then. So we've cleared that up now. Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Briefly, Mr. Manning, can you summarise for the Trial Chamber the types of analyses prepared or performed by Dr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Dr. Brown has detailed in his report specific methods of examination, examining the soil. They refer to methods accepted by geologists and people in that field. I, unfortunately, can't explain those tests, but some of those tests were by using a microscope in and examining the structure of the soil, the structure of fossils within it and particularly in the structure, type, of pollen grains within that soil sample.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Did you conclude that there were similar types of soil found in primary and secondary graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Referring to your report, Prosecutor's Exhibit 140, could you place on the ELMO the page and the chart that is found at 00950927. Using -- we need to lower it a little bit. Using this particular chart, can you inform the Trial Chamber where the soil from primary grave sites matched the soil found in secondary grave sites based on Dr. Brown's analysis?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Using Dr. Brown's analysis, the Branjevo Military Farm soil pollen samples matched that at Cancari Road 12. The Kozluk primary grave matches that at Cancari Road 3. The Glogova 2 grave matches that at Zeleni Jadar 5. And the Orahovac or Lazete grave matches all three at Hodzici Road 3, Hodzici Road 4 and Hodzici Road 5.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Now, there is a small box of soil samples found between the site, the dam and Liplje 2, that was not the subject of Dr. Brown's analysis. That's an analysis performed by another expert; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: We'll get to that testimony later in the course of this trial. That concludes this particular link between primary and secondary grave sites. What I'd like to do now, Mr. Manning, is turn to another source of evidence that linked the primary grave sites to secondary grave sites. Let me ask you, you've testified first of all about finding a large number of cloth ligatures and blindfolds. Were those or some samples of those cloth ligatures that were found in primary sites and in secondary sites submitted to the Netherlands Forensic Institute which is part of the Dutch Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: And was the purpose of that submission to have the Netherlands Forensic Institute make an analysis of the materials that were found in primary and secondary sites to determine if the materials were the same?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to your report, please, Mr. Manning, at page 15/21. Before you place that on the ELMO, let me ask you some questions before we place this on the ELMO. What types of analysis did the Netherlands Forensic Institute conduct on the cloth material samples; can you tell us that after having reviewed their report?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, the investigation was conducted by Ms. Suzie Maljaars who examined the cloths in an attempt to group them into like cloths. She and other scientists examined the cloth for colour, weave, pattern, shininess of the material. It was examined under a microscope to determine the number of threads within the weave, the embroidery pattern, also the elasticity of the material. As a result of that, the cloths were grouped within graves in groups of like cloths, of similar cloths and a simple or a representative sample from each of those groups was compared to the other graves to a representative sample from those other graves.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Did the Netherlands Forensic Institute prepare a final report with their conclusions and did they submit that to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, Judge Wald, the particular report which is the Netherlands Forensic Institute report, Exhibit 143, was filed with the Trial Chamber by the Office of the Prosecutor on the 28th of February 2000. And on the 1st of March 2000, the Defence filed a notice pursuant to Rule 94 bis (B) informing the Trial Chamber that they had accepted that expert report.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Now, if you will, Mr. Manning, turning to your report Prosecutor 140, would you place page 15/21 on the ELMO, and can you please tell us what their conclusions were.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: After examining that report and the details provided by the Dutch lab, they advised that cloth ligatures or blindfolds located at the Branjevo Military Farm matched those at Cancari Road 12. A group of blindfolds or a type of blindfold ligature also matched that at Cancari Road 3. There was no match from Zeleni Jadar 5. Cloth blindfolds collected from the Grbovci school matched those at Hodzici Road 4. Cloth collected from Orahovac Lazete 2 matched all three secondary graves of Hodzici Road 4, 3, and 5. Also, a cloth ligature or blindfold from Hodzici Road 4 matched that at the secondary site of Liplje 2.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Now, let me just ask you to put some examples of the type of the materials that were compared on the ELMO to illustrate the types of materials that were compared. And if you would start by taking Prosecutor's Exhibit 143, please, it's appendix 1, the page number on that, the ERN number is 00916676. Could you place that --

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Sorry Mr. Harmon, I don't have the pages of that report.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: It's the colourful pattern. Do you have the report in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could the registrar please furnish the witness with a copy of that report, 143, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, you're familiar with the report and you're familiar with the exhibit that I'm referring to. Would you please place that on the ELMO. Now earlier, Mr. Manning, we had seen in a picture on a skull that had been exhumed a piece of colourful material. Now, can you explain what this particular exhibit is and its significance?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This exhibit is from the report by Ms. Maljaars. It includes a strip of cloth spread out on the table and photographed. This cloth has a distinctive pattern, a colourful pattern printed on to the material. This piece of cloth and the one below it obviously particularly similar. She examined both of these cloths to the level that I previously described and established that they were indistinguishable from each other. Of particular notice, that this cloth at the bottom is from the Pilica grave, the Branjevo Military Farm grave. This piece of cloth is from the Cancari Road 12 cloth.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Turn to the next exhibit please, Mr. Manning. It is found in appendix 2 at 00916678. Explain this exhibit, please, Mr. Manning.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, this is three strips of cloth spread out on a table to be viewed. They are from three different graves. The top one is the Pilica Branjevo Military Farm primary grave and the other two are from the Cancari Road 12 and Cancari Road 3 secondary graves. Of particular note is not only is the type of cloth colour material the same. These cloths have an embroidered circle with a flower which is quite visible. Each of these cloths has the same embroidered mark on them and, again, they are found to be indistinguishable from each other.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: These samples were found at three different locations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Three different locations, three different graves.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Lastly, let's turn to appendix 3 in Prosecutor's Exhibit 143 at page 00916680. Can you please explain what this exhibit represents?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a view of another type of cloth used as a blindfold or ligature. In this case, blindfolds. These are from two separate graves, but as you can see, the pattern is very similar. There is a clean or straight edge at the bottom. The cloth is of a similar width, and there's a scalloped pattern across the top of the cloth. This particular pattern is seen on a large number of blindfolds and ligatures and is seen at a number of different graves.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Where did these two cloth samples come from, where were they retrieved and what did they link?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Harmon, without referring to the report, itself, and checking those numbers, I can't tell you. I believe the Hodzici Road graves.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: All right. Well, the answer to that question is found in the report, and we'll leave the answer imbedded in that report for further examination if you don't know. Let's -- I've concluded then with that particular exhibit, and we've concluded with the analysis of this particular set of links between primary and secondary graves, Mr. Manning. What I'd like to do now is place Prosecutor's Exhibit 27/7 on the ELMO. We're going to turn our attention, Mr. Manning, to another connection between primary grave site and secondary grave site. We'll start by putting this particular exhibit on the ELMO. We've seen this exhibit earlier in this trial. Mr. Manning, can you tell us what this particular exhibit is?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I recognise this photograph of the Vetinka bottling factory which is located near the Kozluk mass grave.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Was the Vetinka bottle factory located next to a headquarters of any particular military unit in the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Next to the bottling factory was the then barracks of the Drina Wolves.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Did the Vetinka bottle factory have labels that reflected "Vetinka bottle factory"?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Amongst a variety of labels, yes. It had the name Vetinka; it also had the town Kozluk on some labels.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Did it also have bottles that were green glass?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, thousands of green glass bottles.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: How far away was the Vetinka bottle factory and the headquarters of the Drina Wolves from the mass execution site at Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: About 1, 1.5 kilometres along the road that you see in front of that factory.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Now, at the mass execution site at Kozluk, was the site itself, before the executions, used as a grounds where the broken glass was discarded by the factory?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Was it a dump site?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: It was apparent that it was a dumping ground for broken bottles, amongst other things.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: If we could now turn to another exhibit, please, that is, Prosecutor's Exhibit 132/103. This doesn't show up as clearly as I'd hoped on this so you'll have to explain to the Trial Chamber what this particular exhibit illustrates.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a photograph of the exhumation site at Kozluk, in particular detailing body 818. The significance of this photo, however, is the massive bodies here and surrounding them and under them is thousands of green glass bottles. You can see the shape here of the base of a bottle. You can see it here, particularly here, near the yellow arrow, yellow and black arrow. Effectively this whole background here is broken green glass.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Now we're going to put another exhibit on the ELMO. It's Prosecutor's Exhibit 132/99. Mr. Manning, could you tell us what's depicted in this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a photo of artefacts recovered from the Kozluk grave. It's numbered 773A, an artefact. It shows paper labels, bottle labels, which were recovered from that grave. You can see part of "Vetinka," or the spelling of Vetinka. On examination of those labels you can see "Vetinka," and "Kozluk" as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Earlier in your testimony you've testified that the Kozluk primary mass grave site had been disturbed, and we had seen in Prosecutor's Exhibit 1/J/I the trench mark or the gouge mark at that particular location.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Let me ask you, then, Mr. Manning, were similar pieces of green glass and labels similar to what's depicted in Prosecutor's Exhibit 132/99 found at secondary mass grave sites?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. The same green glass, the same labels, were found at the secondary grave of Cincari Road 3.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Let me start then by using the next exhibit, which is 128/263. Would you place that on the ELMO, please. Would you lower that just a little bit, please. Now, what is this exhibit? What does this exhibit depict, Mr. Manning?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This exhibit is an exhumation photo from the secondary grave of Cincari Road 3. It is an individual, a skull, and what is a blindfold fallen from the face. It was given an artefact number. The significance of this particular photo, and again it's not as clear as perhaps hoped, is in the background here are fragments, pieces, of green glass bottles. In the Cincari Road 3 grave, there were thousands of small pieces of glass adhering to the bodies and within the grave itself.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Let's turn to the next exhibit, please, which is 132/101. Mr. Manning, what is depicted in this particular exhibit?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a photograph taken at the mortuary of artefacts recovered from the Cincari Road 3 grave. It's numbered 402. It is the glass labels -- the bottle labels, sorry, "Vetinka" and "Kiseljak Water." But again on those labels was "Vetinka" and "Kozluk."

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: So these labels were found mixed in with the bodies that were discovered at the secondary mass grave at Cincari Road 3.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Let's turn to the last exhibit in this series, Mr. Manning, Prosecutor's Exhibit 132/105. Mr. Manning, what does this particular exhibit depict?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a photograph taken during a trenching operation of the Cincari Road 1 grave by an investigator. What it shows is a body part, in this case a part of the pelvis, within the unexhumed grave of Cincari Road 1. As you can see clearly, again pieces of broken green glass.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: This is a grave that was probed, it wasn't fully exhumed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: All right. Based on your analysis of the findings of green glass and Vetinka bottle labels in the secondary sites of Cincari Road 1 and Cincari Road 3, is it your conclusion that the bodies found in those two sites came from the primary mass execution site at Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Certainly the bodies in Cincari Road 3 came from Kozluk, and I believe that the bodies in Cincari Road 1 will be shown to have come from Kozluk, particularly by the obvious green glass fragments. That will be more clear once it's exhumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Usher, if we could have placed on the easel Prosecutor's Exhibit 135. It's previously been shown.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, if you would prepare, while that's being done, locate in your report page number 00950927 and place that on the ELMO. Mr. Manning, would you approach the large easel exhibit. What I'd like you to do, please, is based on the analyses that we've been discussing, the shell casings, the soil analysis, the textile analysis, the presence of green glass and labels, could you summarise, please, the movement of victims' bodies from primary mass execution and grave sites to secondary sites, based on the analysis and based on the reports that you've reviewed.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. Based on all that material, the bodies from Branjevo Military Farm, the primary grave, were removed from that grave, some of the bodies, and were then transported to Cincari Road 12 where they were placed in that grave. The primary grave site of Kozluk was robbed; some of those bodies were taken and transported to Cincari Road 3. This site at the Dam, near Petkovci, was robbed, with the majority of the bodies being taken to Liplje 2. The site at Orahovac (Lazete 2) was robbed; bodies from that grave were transported to the graves Hodzici Road 3, 5, and 4.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: And Glogova.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Also the primary mass grave of Glogova 2, bodies from that grave were transported to and reburied at Zeleni Jadar 5.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: All right. Have a seat again, Mr. Manning, please. The exhibit that's found on the ELMO, which is from your report at page 00950927, is essentially a summary chart coming to the same conclusions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Essentially, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Manning, we're going to turn to a different topic at this point because I'd like you to discuss some additional forensic reports that were prepared and submitted to the Office of the Prosecutor. Now, following the revelation that mass executions had occurred, did the Office of the Prosecutor send investigators to two locations? First of all, did they send a team of investigators and forensic experts from the United States Naval Investigative Service to the Kravica warehouse, on the 30th of September, 1996?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if we could place on the ELMO Prosecutor's Exhibit 8/4, which is a panorama of the Kravica warehouse.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, is this the location where the experts went? Is this the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's the Kravica warehouse, one end of the warehouse, if you like. They examined this end of the warehouse, to the right of the picture. They didn't examine the far end of the warehouse, depicted on the left.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: What was the purpose of that examination?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: We had been told by witnesses, and there was evidence there, of a mass execution. Their job was to collect evidence to corroborate that witness, or those witnesses, to the fact that there was a major execution that took place in that building.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Did they collect hair and blood samples and explosives residue samples?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: They did, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Did they provide those samples to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Now, let me place on the ELMO a photograph from a report that was prepared by the Naval Investigative Service, Prosecutor's Exhibit 181/1. I'd like you to put on the ELMO, please, Mr. Manning, photograph 16 from roll 2. There are many photographs in this particular report, are there not?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: There are many volumes of reports -- volumes of photos.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: But I have selected one particular photograph just to illustrate the location where samples were taken. That's photograph 16, on the bottom. What is that, please, Mr. Manning?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a photograph of the wall of the warehouse. More particularly, it's a photograph of what is blood, human blood, on the wall, splashed across the wall of the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Just describe briefly how a blood sample was collected.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Using two sampling methods, water and a scraping action, the naval investigators would remove a section of the stain, scrape it off and also swab it off, place it into bags which they sealed and numbered, and the numbering up in the top corner would reflect the number of the sample.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: All right. Those samples were provided to the Office of the Prosecutor for later analysis.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Let's turn our attention to another mass killing site, the Pilica Dom. If I could have Prosecutor's Exhibit 25/7 placed on the ELMO. As a point of reference to your testimony, Mr. Manning, can you tell us what is illustrated in this particular exhibit.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a photograph of the Pilica Dom in or near the town of Pilica. At the rear of this building was the execution point examined by the Naval Investigation Service.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: The Office of the Prosecutor sent investigators to that location after Drazen Erdemovic informed the Prosecutor that approximately 500 Muslims had been executed at that location on the 16th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Now, did the Office of the Prosecutor investigators and Naval Investigative Service forensic specialists go to the Pilica Dom between the 27th and 29th of September, 1996, and did they return again on the 2nd of October, 1996?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Was their purpose similar to the purpose that you've described as those same experts and investigators going to the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Did they, in fact, turn over the hair, blood samples and the explosives residue samples that they collected at the Pilica Dom to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: What I'd like you to do, please, Mr. Manning, is if you would take Prosecutor's Exhibit 181/4, and I'm referring to photograph 18 in roll 10 of that exhibit. I'd like you to just illustrate what an explosives pattern looks like and explain to the Judges how a sample of an explosives residue is collected.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: In this photo you can see there's some markings on the wall, red marks, and some numbering. That's part of the examination process. But in the centre of the photo you see a black staining rising from the floor area. This is soot or residue from an explosives seat which has struck the wall or gone up the wall. The naval investigation service members again number marked that area. They took a swab using water and also a swab using a light acid in separate samples. They then bagged, numbered that, and provided that to the Office of the Prosecutor, from various areas within the Pilica Dom.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Did the Naval Investigative Service prepare a report describing their collection methods, and did they submit that report to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Have you reviewed their report?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President and Judge Wald, in respect of this report, this is Prosecutor's Exhibit 181/1, which is the Naval Investigative report for the Kravica warehouse, and Prosecutor's Exhibits 181/2, /3, and /4, which is the Naval Investigative Service report for the Pilica Dom, these reports were filed by the Office of the Prosecutor, pursuant to Rule 94 bis, on the 2nd -- I'm sorry, on the 7th of February, 2000 and on the 25th of February, 2000, the Defence notified the Trial Chamber in writing, pursuant to Rule 94 bis (B) that she had accepted the reports from the Naval Investigative Service.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Subsequently, Mr. Manning, did the Office of the Prosecutor submit to the Dutch Ministry of Justice, again, the Netherlands Forensic Institute, numerous blood and tissue samples that had been collected by the Naval Investigative Service for an analysis to determine if human DNA was present in those samples?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Why did they submit those samples to the Netherlands Forensic Institute?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Those samples were representative of the blood and tissue on the walls of the buildings. They submitted it in an attempt to corroborate the execution of those people in the buildings.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: In the Pilica Dom and --

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: And Kravica warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President and Judge Wald, the Netherlands Forensic Institute report on the analysis of blood and tissue samples was filed by the Office of the Prosecutor on the 7th of February 2000. And on the 25th of February 2000, the Defence filed written notice pursuant to Rule 94 bis (B) informing the Trial Chamber that they had accepted the reports from the Netherlands Forensic Institute.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Manning, briefly, can you summarise the types of analysis that were performed on the blood and tissue samples by the Netherlands Forensic Institute?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The institute used standard testing methods involving chemical reactions which proved positive to the presence of human DNA. They applied that to all the samples and then produced the report detailing which ones were positive.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to those conclusions, please, Mr. Manning. What were the conclusions of the Netherlands Forensic Institute in respect of the blood and tissue samples from the Pilica Dom. How many samples were submitted and what were their conclusions?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Of the 234 representative blood, hair or tissue samples which were collected throughout the Pilica Dom. They were able to establish that 166 of those samples were positive for the presence of human DNA.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Turning to the samples that had been collected from the Kravica warehouse, how many samples were analysed by the Netherlands Forensic Institute and what were their conclusions?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: From the Kravica warehouse, 149 represented blood, hair or tissue samples were collected throughout the building and the Netherlands Forensic Science Laboratory Institute said that 142 of those samples were said to contain human DNA.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Now the Netherlands Forensic Institute report, Mr. President and Judge Wald, is Prosecutor's Exhibit 150. That's the report relating to the blood and human tissue analysis. The last part of my examination, Mr. Manning, deals with the analysis of the explosives residue that was collected by the Naval Investigative Service and retained -- those samples were retained by the Office of the Prosecutor. Let me ask you first of all: Did the Office of the Prosecutor submit those explosives residue samples to the Netherlands Forensic Institute for an analysis?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Did the Netherlands Forensic Institute conduct an analysis?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Did they prepare a report?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, Judge Wald, the report of the Netherlands Forensic Institute relating to the analysis of explosives residue is Prosecutor's Exhibit 97. That report was filed by the Prosecutor with the Trial Chamber on the 24th of March 2000. I may have the wrong date on that. I apologise. It was -- all I can say in looking at my notes is that it was filed by the Office of the Prosecutor, I'm sorry, on the exact date, but on the 24th of February, 2000, the Defence filed a written notice pursuant to Rule 94 bis (B) informing the Trial Chamber that they had accepted the conclusions of that report.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Could you please, Mr. Manning, summarise, first of all, the types of analysis that the Institute conducted on the samples of residue explosives residue that had been submitted to them?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: In relation to the explosives analysis, I'm not able to describe what these are, but it was a reversed-phase high-performance liquid chromatography and photo-diode array detection test and confirmed using a reversed-phase high-performance liquid chromatography and double mass-spectrometry detection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd like to hear the translation of that. I think that's probably pretty tough to translate, but we appreciate the effort.

utterances.speaker: THE ATF
utterances.text: Any event, Mr. Manning without going into the scientific analysis would you just tell us what their conclusions were?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Effectively they informed me that their conclusion were that of the 15 representative samples of explosive residue collected throughout the Pilica Dom, a single sample was found to be positive for the presence of the high explosive TNT. And in relation to the Kravica warehouse, 23 of the representative samples of explosive residue were examined, two were found to have possible traces of TNT, the high explosive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, thank you very much. I've concluded my direct examination. Your Honours, I've concluded my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Visnjic or Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has reviewed the report of the expert as Prosecution Exhibit 140. This exhibit was disclosed to the Defence three days prior to today. Bearing in mind the report of Mr. Manning and the fact that it is really a summary report of other reports that will be reviewed here in the courtroom in the next few days, and bearing in mind the very short time that we have had, and the fact that the text was received only in the English version, the Defence, in the interest of uninterrupted, positive cooperation with the Prosecution, the Defence has taken the liberty to suggest to the Prosecution that the cross-examination of Mr. Manning, if possible, if the Prosecution agrees, and if Mr. Manning can come back, should be held in the middle of next week after the other expert witnesses have been heard, according to the plan of witnesses, because a part of the questions which might be addressed to Mr. Manning after today's examination-in-chief will be put to the other expert witnesses and thereby the cross-examination of Mr. Manning would be shorter. That is why I should like to suggest to the Chamber, to accept this motion of ours, and to allow us to postpone the cross-examination until the middle of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have discussed this with my colleagues, Mr. President. I have no objection to that. The only request that I have is that there is presently in place a court order that I cannot contact or communicate with my witnesses. Mr. Manning and I may have a need to discuss matters other than his testimony. I have no intention of discussing his testimony with him, but I would ask to be relieved of the order of the Court saying that I cannot contact Mr. Manning. What I would request is that on matters other than his testimony, I be permitted to talk to him about other matters relating to the investigation. That also would apply to members of my trial team as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no objections to that, we have no objections to that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, we are going to show confidence in Mr. Harmon, who may talk to Mr. Manning regarding other matters, but not regarding this case. Is that acceptable, Mr. Harmon and Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, we are going to trust you. Mr. Manning has heard well what we have decided regarding this matter. So exceptionally, we will suspend the ruling of the Chamber. We will treat this as an exception so that Mr. Harmon may contact the witness, but not on this subject. As to the request of Mr. Visnjic, the Chamber fully understands your reasons and I think that from the point of view of the rights of the accused to a fair and expeditious trial, I think it is good to combine fairness with efficiency so that we will have the cross-examination in the middle of next week. Do you have a more or less fixed date? Is the witness available?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Manning is available all of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What are we going to do next, Mr. Harmon? Are we going to have an expert witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, I think you had some remarks to make or certain suggestions regarding that so please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, our suggestion and request to the Trial Chamber would be that during the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination of expert witnesses that the Prosecutor is going to call, that the Defence be allowed to include, on the Defence team, our own expert so that he might assist the Defence counsel with his expert knowledge of terms and the subject matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, bearing in mind your request, Mr. Visnjic, and the fact that the Prosecutor has no objection but also in line with Article 90, paragraph D, the Chamber allows the presence of your expert so as to help you in preparing for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The last item I have, Mr. President, is I would request that the exhibits that have been tendered in the direct examination of Mr. Manning be introduced at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, have you any objection to the admission of the exhibits mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, the Prosecution exhibits are admitted into evidence. I think there are no other matters to deal with before the break, so we are now going to have a break, and we will be able to resume with the expert witness' testimony, and I should like to ask the registrar to have the witness brought in before we begin so as to speed things up. It is now five to 1.00. I think that we can have a 20-minute break now. I can feel that there are many people who would like a half an hour break. I think we need to work for at least an hour and a quarter, so let's have a 25-minute break. A 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that we ended up having a half-hour break, but never mind. I see that the two parties are standing up. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Good afternoon. Good afternoon, Judge Wald, Mr. Visnjic. Professor Wright is our next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Visnjic, perhaps you could take advantage of this opportunity to introduce your expert witness whom we see in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you. I was just going to do so. With us we have Docent Dr. Zoran Stankovic, the head of the Institute for Forensic Medicine of the Medical Military Academy in Belgrade. Mr. Stankovic is on the list of experts of the United Nations for forensic medicine and has been there since 1964. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. May I say welcome to Mr. Zoran Stankovic. I'm now going to turn to Professor Wright and say good afternoon to him. Can you hear me, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are now going to read the solemn declaration that the usher is going to give you. Please go ahead, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Perhaps you are already acquainted with procedure. For the moment, Professor, you're going to answer questions put to you by the Prosecutor, Mr. Peter McCloskey. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Prior to addressing Professor Wright, I would like to -- as a point of background, as we've heard, he was the supervising archaeologist for our exhumations of 1998 and 1999, and we have filed, in November 1999, which is Exhibit 204, his report for the 1998 exhumations, and Exhibit 205, which we filed on February 18th of 2000, is his report on the 1999 exhumations. We were notified by the Defence that they would like to cross-examine Professor Wright. So we are calling Professor Wright to give you some of the background and some more of the scientific detail of the exhumations, though, as we can all imagine, this could be a subject of several months of a course. We will try to keep it to the highlights and to the brief points, but of course he'll be open for everyone's questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Professor Wright, could you state your name and spell your last name for the record.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. My name is Richard Wright, and the spelling of my surname is W-r-i-g-h-t.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I'm an archaeologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us a review of your educational background and your employment background.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. I was educated at Cambridge University, where I have a masters degree. I was employed in the Anthropology Department of the University of Sidney in 1961, and in 1981 I had the Chair of Anthropology, which I held until 1990. I resigned from that position in 1990 and the university gave me the title of Emeritus Professor of Anthropology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We should remember we need -- everything we've said is being translated so we need to, probably both of us, slow down a little bit, and it's something that we may be reminded of as we go. In any event, can you briefly describe to us what the field of archaeology is and in particular how it fits in to the exhumations of mass graves.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. From the point of view of these investigations, archaeologists are experts in the recognition of disturbed soil; in recovering objectives, whether they're bodies or artefacts, from that disturbed soil; in properly recording the location of objectives from that disturbed soil. That's the central expertise of archaeologists. This expertise is required for the detection and exhumation of mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How does that fit in to the greater picture of archaeology that you were taught and learned in school and practised before that? Just briefly, how is it related to the classic archaeology, as we speak.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I think the aspects of archaeology that I've mentioned are absolutely central to the discipline; that is, the use of soil to reveal what went on in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does an archaeologist analyse artefacts and soil together to try to build a picture of the dig, what it means, what happened, what the various things might tell us about a prior culture, or in this case a prior crime?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly the responsibility of archaeologists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In fact, you did do that in your exhumations for the OTP.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us a background in some of the exhumations, archaeological work that you've done in the past, perhaps starting in your earlier years and working around.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: My general or my major interest has been in the archaeology of Australia, particularly the excavation of sites that have bones from marsupials, and trying to reconstruct the environment from those sites. In 1990 I began to develop a special interest in forensic investigations, and I was employed by the Australian government to investigate three mass graves in the Ukraine. That was in 1990 and 1991. Before I worked for the Prosecutor, I worked on the recovery of human remains in the Middle East, that was an archaeological job, and I also worked for the New South Wales investigators for the recovery of the skeletons of children from a nineteenth century orphanage cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit more about your archaeological dig in the Ukraine? Who was that for? And can you just describe briefly about that dig.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, the Australian government had complaint made to it that three naturalized Australians had participated in the killing of large number of Jews in 1942. The war crimes investigation unit in Sydney asked me whether I would go over there to see whether there were graves, where the eyewitnesses said there were graves and whether they contained the remains of the sort that the eyewitnesses had stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you able to go over at that time, the Soviet Union and do an exhumation of a mass grave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, in 1990 I conducted the exhumations at Serniki which contained 550 mainly women and children who had been shot in the head. In 1991, I went to Ustinovka which is in the Ukraine and conducted the excavations at a grave where adults had been killed first and then children. And later in 1991, I conducted the exhumation of a grave at Gnivan, also in the Ukraine, where about 100 victims had been shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And these were Jewish victims?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: These were Jewish victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In those graves were you able to find artefacts like paper materials and things that you've been able to since recover in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: We were able to find -- I don't remember papers specifically, because these were extremely old sites and papers had disintegrated, but we were able to find shell cases that had the date and manufacture of -- manufactured in Germany in 1939, 1941, and 1942.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you try to prove ethnicity or background in those graves as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, we didn't -- that wouldn't have been my responsibility anyway, but the -- my responsibility was that of an archaeologist. But the point of the -- whole point of the work was to establish whether the eyewitnesses' testimony had any credibility. In other words, whether the material evidence supported the claims of the eyewitnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, before we get into your ICTY experience, I notice that you refer to yourself as an archaeologist. The front of your report refers to you as a professor of anthropology, and we have already heard about forensic pathologists from the summary witnesses. Can you tell us what forensic anthropology is, where you fit in that field and how it fits into the field of archaeology and exhumations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, put very simply, in this sort of work there are three disciplines that are called on; one of that is archaeology, and I've described the reasons why archaeologists are called in to do this work in connection with the soils. The anthropological side concerns the study of the bones for the purpose of determining the sex and age of the individual, and interpreting breaks and other holes in the bones. In addition, the pathologists, who are drawn from the medical profession, are the ones who finally determine the cause and manner of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, when you deliver, your team delivers all these broken up bones to the morgue, which profession is it that tries to sort out the minimum number of individuals based on the --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: The anthropologists do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when did you first start working for the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: In June 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you just briefly describe what your work involved?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I was in charge of the exhumations at Brcko where there were Muslim and Croatian victims.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: In 1998, I worked for the case that we are discussing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As well as 1999?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: As well as 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this year are you continuing to work for the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I've just completed an investigation in Croatia where there are alleged Serb victims, and I'm currently working at Prijedor in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, the first exhumation you began with in 1998 for the Srebrenica team was the dam; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we have a film, as you're aware, of an exhumation at Cancari 12, so I'm going to take us out of order, briefly, and we'll play that film a bit later. Starting with Cancari 12, can you tell the Court a little bit about what you knew about the area going into it, and what you first did when you came to the area, what plan you developed.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, the plans are essentially the same for all the sites. The ICTY investigators take me to a place where they suspect there is a mass grave. Often, their knowledge comes from aerial imagery. I then have to find the exact location of the grave within the generally disturbed area. I then take charge of the finding of the grave, the removal of the bodies and the putting of the bodies into a freezer van which is then sent to the mortuary and my duty stops with sending the bodies down to the mortuary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do the investigators many times investigate the surface of the area if there appears to be evidence or indications of the crime prior to you coming on it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Sometimes yes and sometimes not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And of course the demining act is the absolutely first thing that happened?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. The area is checked for mines and booby traps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we've seen a clip of the beginning of the Cancari 12 site of surveyors and of a backhoe at work, and you're walking around, and we'll get to that very soon. But can you just tell us before we get into that, what's going on there, what are your plans, what's going on there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: We, when I say "we", I mean the team of experts which includes archaeologist and anthropologists under my direction, we use a backhoe, a mechanical backhoe to find the exact location of the grave. Our task is not to find bodies first, but to find the outline of the grave, and that way we do the least damage to the remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe your team? Can you give us more detail on who is working with you and what kind of work they do?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: The team of archaeological and anthropological consists normally of about ten people. They're drawn from literally all over the world. We depend a lot on experts from Central and South America who have to investigate police and military killings in their own countries. And they sometimes have archaeological expertise, sometimes anthropological expertise, but many people have both.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is with an educational background to back it up. And do you have just basic labourers, you know, there is this -- there may be ideas out there that from films that there is labourers running around. Who are basically the labourers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: The experts may look like labourers when they're doing the work but we don't have local labourers. The people who do the work are the experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So the people we'll see in the film are all educated experts in their field of archaeology or anthropology by and large?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, and by and large they'll -- well, they've already done forensic work before ICTY takes them on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could start with the tape. We have three or four minutes of the tape that you've seen before. But then we'll get into the end of the tape that you did not see before and, Dr. Wright, if you could explain some of the things that are going on in it and I may stop the tape to give you a better chance to explain more detail. So if we dim the lights and play Exhibit 188

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: This is the site of Cancari 12, as you see, a secondary grave. Here my experts are setting up a surveying system to record the grave itself and the contents of the grave. The backhoe will be used to scrape off the surface of the soil until we are satisfied that we have the complete outline of the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How do you do that without messing up the potential evidence there? This seems like a big machine.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: They are removing only the top of the grave. The driver that we have has been doing forensic work since 1996, so he's familiar with the changes of colour and texture in the soil that has to be established. We also have to clear a large area around the grave, so some of these pictures that look as though destruction is taking place are due to the clearing of a large area outside the grave. The soil here, I should say, is a clay. Most of these graves are in what's called a loess soil which is a brownish clay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say "these graves" are you referring to the secondary graves or all the graves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: All except the dam site which is in a construction --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What are you doing here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Here what we think are the outlines of the grave are being marked with flags.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we stop the film right here, please. Go ahead, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Here you can see the natural soil, I don't think my pointer shows on this, does it? At the top of the picture, you can see the brownish soil and we're beginning to see now the blueish-green soil which is characteristic of these clays when they've been in contact with putrefying bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe that you're referring to the little orange -- the second orange piece from the top you can see a dark clay to the left and a blueish clay to the right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: The band across the middle of the picture is the blueish clay that we use to detect where bodies are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And that's what you are marking with the little tags?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What do those little indicate? What are you marking there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: We are here developing the outline of the rectangular grave. This is a very early stage when we were still exploring to find the whole outline of the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How do you know that this colour change in the soil actually outlines a grave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: In my experience in Bosnia, when we find this greenish soil near the surface, it's invariably in contact with putrefying bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just feel free to comment as we go along.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: And here you can see the development of what we suspect in the early stages to be the outline of the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did that turn out to be correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You trust your backhoe driver.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Normally. And then there is some development of the detail by hand. In this case, one of my experts using a pick.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How much of the work actually gets done by backhoe?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Very little, just the development of the outline of the grave and the putting in of a ditch around the grave itself to control flood water and to give us access to the bodies. So all that we're looking at is not exhumation but the preparatory work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as yet you haven't found any indication of human remains aside from the colour in soil; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: At Cancari 12, we did find some bones on the surface, but here we see the first remains, some bones. At the top left, a shoe, on the right, and this characteristic greenish soil. And at this stage, we have the whole of the outline of the Cancari Road 12 grave visible and on the left, you can see the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Stop here. Excuse me, Professor. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: On the left-hand side, you can see a deep trench which is artificial in the sense that we have put that deep trench in, and on the centre and to the right is the -- are the contents of the grave itself. So the grave is turned into a mound by putting trenches around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So it be -- the perimeter of the grave does -- it is not included in this ditch that you're talking about, it's only the area, the mound we see?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: The perimeter of the grave is what the experts are working on to reveal bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: So the work consists of -- the removal of the empty soil and once the bodies are exposed then we use trowels and sometimes brushes. Here is a much later stage of the work. People are walking in the trench and they are surveying --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Stop this again, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: They are surveying the bodies within the grave. We --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, for each of the bodies, we record 12 landmarks; the skull, the shoulders, the elbows, the wrists, the pelvis, the knees, and the ankles. And that allows us to reconstruct the arrangement of bodies within the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this surveying system is an electronic system that actually records these various points?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. It records the number of metres north, number of metres east and the depth of each of the points, it's a three dimensional recording system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: A little later on, we'll see some of the results of the surveying system. Continue with the film, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: This is the surveying process in place, taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you see some investigators working along with your team there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to the archaeological/anthropological experts, we have working at the site police, as scene-of-crime officers, and we have investigators from ICTY who are really observers of what's going on at the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What's going on here with these numbers and the labelling of these bones?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: We assign a unique number to each body or body part found within the grave. Here they have recovered a hand with a ligature, cloth ligature, and that is being bagged separately, because in the secondary graves we often find just an arm or a hand that's been ripped off at the time of removing the bodies from the primary graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the process of photography.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. Each of these items is photographed and a log is kept of the photographs and cross-referred to the site log. "A," as you see there, signifies an artefact that's being photographed. Here the hand with the ligature is being bagged and will be sent down to the morgue for further analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That will be the anthropologists' work; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Anthropologists, and investigators in the morgue. There's a scene-of-crime officer in the middle and one of the anthropologists on the left. The remains, the human remains, are put in body bags and these are taken to the chiller van and periodically transferred down to the ICTY morgue, which is in Visoko. This is one of the body sheets, the record sheets --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we stop there so we can explain that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Each time we remove a virtually complete body, the experts fill out a form that describes the properties of this body, the way in which it's lying, whether it shows any signs of injury, whether it has clothing, and so on. So this form that you're seeing here is a checklist to be sure that the excavators have recorded critical information, and these forms are sent to the morgue with the bodies for the information of the mortuary staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Continue, please. Is this the typical kind of checklist that you would do on many archaeological projects?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. The surveying is continuing here. The person holding the staff communicates with a surveyor by means of a two-way radio because of the noise of machinery in the distance. Here you can see someone filling out one of these body sheets. Here some remains are obviously being put into the body bag.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How do the archaeologists sort out what part belongs to what body?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: In the case of primary graves that have not been disturbed, that's very easy. But in the case of secondary graves, they will follow an arm or a leg until it stops, or the next bone makes no anatomical sense, and so they will call that a body part and it will be sent to the morgue, and I understand some attempt to link these pieces together is made at the morgue. But because these are secondary graves and the bodies have been ripped out of the primary graves, everything is mixed up. So the fact that two body parts are found together is not a necessary indication that they belong together. It's a complicated process of reconstruction. In a sense, what's happening now is the end of my responsibilities as a team leader. The bodies have been put into the chiller van, and then the anthropological and pathological analysis starts at the morgue later. Here the individuals are searching the outside of the body for any documents, looking in the outside clothing. The reason for doing that is that oxygen, to which these bodies are now freshly exposed, can cause rapid deterioration of images and so we take photographs of any documents that are on the outside of the bodies. Those that are on the inside are much more protected from oxygen and so we let the people in the morgue discover those in the course of their pathological examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is this the chiller van you spoke of?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. Here are the bags, the body bags, waiting for transmission to the morgue. This van is locked, and the scene-of-crime officers are responsible for maintaining the chain of custody. Here you see a shell case mixed up with the bodies. These are treated as artefacts and are put in evidence bags and then sent down with the bodies to the morgue, where the investigators take over. They are cleaned with a toothbrush and water in order to prevent any further corrosion of the cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: These are largely brass cases.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's a computer. Do you have computers out there? And could we stop just briefly, could we stop it, please. Can you explain where the computer fits in.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. We have two systems of maintaining the log. The log of the site which lists all the bodies and their properties -- their sequence numbers is kept on paper, and at the end of the day, for security reasons, to ensure we don't lose the thing, the paper log is typed into a computer version of the log.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Continue. Thank you. You can continue.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Here is an example of one of the documents found at Cancari 3 which was photographed and on which you can see a name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Salko Ramic.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Salko Ramic, information about --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mother, Sabin --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, and where it was issued. And then this -- although this is not my work, it's an example of some preliminary work that's done at the site by the investigators to see whether the names on the documents that my team recovers also occur in this missing persons register.
