This is the missing persons register with the same name as the person that was on the document that my team recovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. That's the end of the film. Professor Wright, now we're going to go back in time a bit to where you first began, and that was at the site known as the dam.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If Professor Wright could be shown Exhibit 22/3, or if he's got that in front of him, we could place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does this photograph reflect the dam before you began work?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, this is the dam before we began work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What can you tell us about the area on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: The suspect area that I've been showing from aerial imagery is circled in red here. It was evident by the growth of weeds that were not growing elsewhere on the dam -- I should say that this whole surface here is an apron in front of the dam, it's entirely artificial ground made up of rocks to contain the dam wall, that is, behind where the photographer is standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Could we move that sideways a bit, going in the -- yes, in that direction. Could you stop right there. Did you at some point wander around a bit and look at some of the piles of rocks in the area and notice anything in particular?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. As an archaeologist I look at all rocks, and I looked at this heap here and decided that it is a demolished mosque; decided that on the basis of the carved stone, angular carved stone, of the sort that I've seen in the structure of mosques. But this, I should say, is well before the killing events that we were investigating because it appears on aerial photographs before the executions took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can you just tell us a bit about this exhumation, what it involved, what you found out about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. The ICTY investigators who took me to the site told me that this was an undisturbed primary grave. I had to tell them very soon into our investigations that this was not an undisturbed primary grave, that it was a robbed primary grave from which bodies had been taken away. What was left after the grave had been filled were many pieces torn off bodies. We were obviously looking at a few dozen people -- the remains of a few dozen people but entirely disintegrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you explain in a little more detail how you knew it was not a primary grave? What were the main characteristics?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: The main characteristics were that there wasn't a complete single body, scarcely a complete limb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you get results back from the anthropologists about how many total individuals were reflected in all these body pieces that you refer to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, may I refer to my notes for numbers and dates and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I may have misspoke if I said how did you know that this was not a primary grave, I should have said how did you know that it was not a primary undisturbed grave, just to clarify the record.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: The same answer would apply, that it consisted of just fragments of human remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe the grave itself, how big it was.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: You asked me just now about the numbers, and I didn't answer it. I asked the President whether I could refer to some notes on this matter that I have with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Professor, naturally. We are not computers that can remember all the dates and the numbers, so please do.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: As I said, I knew that there were some tens of people here. The report that I have seen from the analysis by the anthropologists at the morgue show that these fragmentary remains account for a minimum number of 46 individuals that were left -- whose pieces were left behind in this primary grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then I'll get back to the question that I asked originally. About how big was this grave? Can you describe what it looked like, and then we'll go on to another exhibit to help that out.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. It was a very large grave. My estimates are is it was 25 metres long, 6 metres broad, and 3 metres deep.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Any indication from the soils or from what you'd seen as to what kind of implement was used to dig this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: We found traces of machine teeth within the grave, showing, not surprisingly, that it was dug by an excavator.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you take a look at what is Exhibit 189. It should be your next in order. Could you please, and thank you, put that on the ELMO. If you could, tell us what this is and --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: This is the grave at the dam, after we have removed the refilling of the grave. It was dug out, the bodies were taken away, and then it was refilled. So we were removing the refilling, and for scale you can see people up here and the vans. So it's a very large trench after we finished removing all the forensic evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you just tell us roughly how long it takes you to get this far? You don't need exact dates. Just a rough number of days.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I can give you the exact number of days that the exhumation there took place: It was ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we look at the next exhibit, which is 190. What is this, and how is it in relation to the last exhibit?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: In the last exhibit you'll remember that there was a bottom to the grave. These are fragments of human remains, that is, bones, scattered along the bottom of the grave, representing what was there after the bodies had been removed and before the grave was refilled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Could we go to Exhibit 191, the next one. What does this represent?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: It represents some clothing contained within the refilling of the robbed grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would that be the kind of clothing that would have been searched like we've seen on the movie?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, it would have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go to the next photo. Now, I note in the bottom this says, "Item 122 from body pocket 028." The previous exhibit was marked, in the photograph, as 028. What is this exhibit, this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: This is a document that my team found in the pocket of that body part that you saw in the previous picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What about these records lead you to believe that, that this came from that, aside from the matching numbers? The numbers at the bottom of this exhibit, is that something your team would have written down?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: The photographer would have written it down before he took the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then it would have been put in the photo log.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: The entry would have been made in the photo log as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. While it cannot be read very well, the name on the exhibit, on the paper was Dzevad Kardasevic. Again, if we could go to the next exhibit, 193. As we've seen in the film, here is a page out of the ICRC missing list with an individual's name in it like that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Now, while we recall those big rocks and boulders from the exhibit of that big hole, as you went through the summer exhuming the various secondary graves, did you come across any of the secondary graves that resembled the rocks from the dam?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. The rocks at the dam are rocks that were used to construct the dam itself, and these were quarried from limestone quarry and have angular edges, as all quarry rocks do. Naturally, when I was looking at secondary graves I was looking out for such angular limestone blocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the Liplje grave, and I may be skipping out of order a bit, but it's Exhibit 194, which should --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, this is the totally exhumed -- this photograph is taken at the grave of Liplje 2 which was totally exhumed, and you can see in various places limestone blocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are those the same kind of rocks as the dam?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: They are the same kind of rocks as the dam, and moreover they are not rocks that are found naturally in the area -- not found naturally in the soil from which the grave was dug.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You inspected the whole area and didn't see any of those cut limestone rocks in that area.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: That's correct. We don't merely inspect the surface of the area, we also inspect, as you can see here, a dug trench through the soils in the area. So we see right down to below the area of the grave, and angular limestone blocks are not to be found in that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how about the contents of the grave? How did you find the contents of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: At Liplje, in particular?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: At Liplje, in particular, the bodies were almost entirely broken up into their individual bones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how did you account for that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I think at the dam itself where the original bodies were mixed up with very large boulders, that as they were removing, as they were robbing the primary grave, the bodies were torn apart by the machinery that was dragging them out. One end of the body being trapped under a boulder, and then the part that's been pulled is separated. Now, I also account for it on the grounds that this -- at the dam site, the soil is fairly porous. Oxygen gets in and speeds up putrefaction, so the periosteal tissues that hold bones together would be partly putrefied and thus the bodies would come apart fairly easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell how many bodies were pulled out of the Liplje site and tell us the exact number of the Liplje site, if you could, that we're looking at?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: This is only the Liplje 2. I had only the vaguest of ideas how many bodies might be represented by these disintegrating body parts, but I was told by the morgue that the minimum number of individuals at this Liplje 2 site was 192.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, let's go back to Cancari Road now. How many bodies were recovered from the Cancari 12 site?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: From the Cancari 12 site, the morgue told me that 177 were recovered by my team.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, the Hodzici sites. Can you tell us about the sites along the Hodzici site?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: The numbers or the properties in general?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, the properties in general. Were they any different as compared to the other secondary sites?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, there was a consistency of size and shape of these secondary sites. They were generally 13 metres long by 3 metres wide by 1.5 to 2 metres deep. The -- except for the Zeleni Jadar secondary site, all the sites had been dug by what I call a front loader, an excavator and we found traces of the wheels and the teeth of those machines in the bottom of the -- in the bottom of the grave. The Hodzici sites and the Cancari Road sites and the Liplje sites were as graves, as dug graves virtually identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could you look at Exhibit 200, I'm sorry, I've skipped again on you it's the bulldozer. And could we put that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. This is not a bulldozer. This is what I was calling a front loader. It's a machine which has obviously got wheels and a bucket at the front and this is the machine -- the marks that we found in the secondary graves along Cancari Road and Hodzici Road and at Liplje are consistent with the graves having been dug by this sort of machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And briefly, on the Hodzici Road sites, can you tell us the numbers of those graves in each, how many bodies came out of those three sites?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. Hodzici Road 3, I was told 40; Hodzici Road 4, 81; Hodzici Road 5, 57.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So while the size of the Hodzici Road graves in -- was almost identical to the size in Cancari Road and Liplje, there is a significantly less number of bodies in those than you had described in Cancari?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: The smaller number of bodies along Hodzici Road, in particular in Hodzici Road 3, as it was a full-sized grave, only had 40 individuals. And Hodzici Road 1 is a grave that was never used at all. That is, the rectangular hole there with all the properties but the hole was not used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: From your exhumations of the secondary graves, were you able to make any kind of estimate on how many truckloads it may have taken or how many truckloads it takes to fill up a grave or was that ever attempted by you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I didn't attempt that because I wouldn't know the size of the trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go to Cancari 3, and can you describe at Cancari 3, as the dig commenced, was its size any different than the others?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, Cancari 3 was a perfectly average-sized secondary grave; that is, it was 12 metres long, 3 metres broad and 2 metres deep.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you note about the geology and the artefacts that was particularly interesting and different from the graves that you saw?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: The grave was dug into clay, but the contents of the grave consisted of river cobbles or pebbles as they are called and some clay, but the most conspicuous artefact mixed up with the bodies in Cancari Road 3 were thousands of fragments of broken green glass.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in particular, what could you tell what the glass was originally or what it had been originally?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, we used our archaeological minds here, if I can just give an account of the properties of these bottles, they were broken. About half of them had the crown seals, the metal seals on the top, so we formed the conclusion that they had been filled before they were broken. None of the bottles had a label on the body of the bottle, and so it appeared to us that they had been broken in some accident in a bottling factory, not in a distribution warehouse, because then you would expect them to have labels as well as their tops. So towards the end of the excavation, we found a large collection, some 100 or 200 labels all stuck together which gave the name Vetinka bottling factory and the town of Kozluk. So I contacted the investigators at ICTY and asked about a primary grave at Kozluk and was told that no investigations had been made there, but Mr. Ruez came down to Bosnia very quickly and we went to Kozluk, passed the Vetinka bottling factory and found an area where there was broken green glass lying around and many hundreds of thousands of fragments and area where holes had been dug and two legs on the surface and some clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that is what we now call the Kozluk primary site that was the subject of your exhumation last year?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, in 1998 we simply observed that there were human remains on the surface there, and in 1999, we carried out an investigation at that site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Then let me go back to Cancari 3 and what were the total numbers that came out of Cancari 3?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Cancari 3, the estimated minimum number of individuals is at 160.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, if I could direct your attention to the exhibits of computer-generated exhibits beginning with 196, and if you could just go through each of the exhibits, 196, 197, 198, and 199 and describe to us, if you could, what -- how you were able to get these images and what actual size they are and how they relate to the various secondary graves you exhumed.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: If we put on one side the top one which is the red dam, I'll just explain briefly how these are constructed. The outlines of the grave when we have finished removing the contents are surveyed by my archaeological surveyor, and from that survey data, the contour image of the grave is constructed. So for each of the graves we do we have such an image. In case of the Cancari 12 site, the dimensions of the Cancari 12 site are 13 metres long by -- 13 metres in this direction, 3 metres broad and 2 metres deep. And you can also, if I can also draw attention to the fact that we can also detect in our excavations the entrance ramp that the front loader went down to excavate the grave. And we frequently find impressions of the wheel marks and the teeth of the impressions of the tines or teeth on the front of the bucket.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll ask you, in particular, when we get to Kozluk on that point, so save that thought. Do we see a ramp on the dam as well? I think you mentioned it in previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, we see a ramp here. Down which were strewn many body parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay and going to the next exhibit, 198.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: At the top, we have the outlines of the Hodzici Road 5 site that I mentioned. The dimensions of the Hodzici Road 5 site 16 metres long by 3 metres by 1.5 metres deep and, again, we have the entrance ramp visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Hodzici 4?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Hodzici 4 has an entrance ramp and Hodzici 4 is 12 metres long by 3 metres long by 1.5 metres deep.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the next exhibit, 199, Liplje 2.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Liplje 2 is the site that I conclude came from the dam, where the bodies came from the dam, and it is 13 metres long by 3 metres wide by 1.5 metres deep and again has an entrance ramp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Zeleni 5?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Zeleni 5 is south of Srebrenica and this is the only grave that was not dug by a front loader. It has no ramp. This appears to be a -- perhaps a ramp but it isn't. It has no whole tracks or tooth marks. I believe that this grave was dug by a backhoe; that is, a machine with an arm that can dig. The dimensions of the Zeleni Jadar 5 site are 17 metres long by 3 metres broad by 1.5 metres deep.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how many bodies came out of the full exhumation of the Zeleni site?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Zeleni site, 150.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So aside from what you've just described as remarkably similar in size than the ones that are much further north?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, did you examine Zeleni 2 in any fashion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I did examine Zeleni 2 because the investigators had asked that I should exhume it, but I had to tell them after my investigations that if it was a secondary grave, and I believe from the aerial imagery that it was a secondary grave that coincided in time with the rest, that that secondary grave had, itself, subsequently been dug out. So somewhere there must be a tertiary grave that we haven't discovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you did to Zeleni 2 that allowed you to reach that conclusion, what you saw?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: There was just a few disconnected human remains and isolated items of clothing in the filling of the Zeleni Jadar 2 grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you able to make out that it was a similar size as the other -- of the other graves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. It was a rectangular structure the same size as the Zeleni Jadar 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Any indications -- was it in any particular area near a stream that was causing any overflow into that grave; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: There was a stream nearby but I don't know whether it would overflow into the grave. It was a very wet area so possibly it would, but I couldn't say for sure that it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, aside from all of those -- how many of the secondary graves did you actually fully exhume? We just went over those.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: We fully exhumed seven secondary graves in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you go on to examine other sites that were believed to be secondary graves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. The investigators took me to places where aerial imagery suggested that they were secondary graves, and these we subjected to a process that we called probing. Probing means within the disturbed area that is shown on the aerial imagery, to try and find the rectangle of the grave, and having done that, to establish that there are multiple body parts within -- multiple bodies, I should say, within the grave. And that's the end of the probing process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you go to the various sites along the Cancari Road, the Hodzici Road, Liplje, and Zeleni Jadar and examine another many sites? And can you tell us how many you examined?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. I examined exactly 21 sites that proved to be secondary -- that proved to be graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, did you, as an archaeologist, make any kind of estimate of numbers of potential bodies inside those unexhumed, yet confirmed secondary graves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I did do that. I did it on the grounds that the secondary graves, the seven that we did exhume along the three roads that we've already discussed, were the same size and shape. What I did was to average the number of bodies found in those seven graves and extend that average to the 21 places that we had probed and shown to have multiple body parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your total for that was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, it's an estimate; that in the 21 graves, based on the seven exhumed graves, in the 21 graves my estimate was 2,571 bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you take the graves by road, in the vicinities, for example, Cancari 12, take the average there, and Hodzici Road, take the average there, and take the average of Zeleni and Liplje, do you come up with a somewhat different number?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. The number of 2,571 takes the whole area of secondary graves as a whole, and that's the number that I gave in my report. If I do it road by road, that is, average the numbers for Cancari Road and then for Hodzici Road, I come up with a higher number. The estimate then would be 3,189 as opposed to the 2,571 that comes from taking the area as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: These are clearly estimates. What's your opinion on the reliability of these estimates for numbers in the ground?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: It's a common archaeological practice to expand one's estimates to unexcavated places from excavated places. Whether or not my estimate is correct could be established by the total exhumation of the graves. But it's, I think, a conservative approach to take the average and then extend it to the other graves. The real number might be less, it might be more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, he has one more grave, primary grave, Kozluk to discuss. It's 2.30. It might be a good time to take a break, so we could start on that on Monday. Or he can go on longer and it shouldn't take us much longer to get through Kozluk, though there are some exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would be ready but I think it is quite impossible to continue today. It is Friday, people have already packed their suitcases, and it would be torture for them to continue the hearing. So for today we'll end there and we will resume work on Monday, at 9.30, won't we.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Professor. Enjoy your weekend here in The Hague. You will be able to take a walk and take a rest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry, one thing. If we could have Dr. Wright -- Professor Wright is in our team area, and if we could have again permission to speak to him on non-testimonial matters. I don't expect to have to speak to him but it's inevitable that I would run into him in the hallways and things, as well as the rest of the team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no objection to this exception.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but with too many exceptions we won't have a rule. We understand that the professor is here for a long weekend and perhaps we should give permission for contact. But I have confidence in you so it's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
